# How to use this guide

Nursing Foundation I (including the First Aid module) is a first-semester course of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum: 6 credits of theory (120 hours), with 80 hours of skill lab and 160 hours of clinical practice in medical and surgical wards. It is the base of everything you will do on the wards — vital signs, infection control, bed making, positioning, admission and discharge, moving patients and first aid.

## There is no university exam for this course this semester

**Read this first.** Nursing Foundation I has **no end-semester university examination in the first semester**. In the first semester you earn only **internal marks**: 25 for theory (10 continuous assessment + 15 sessional exams) and 25 for practical. These internal marks are **carried forward** and added to the internal marks of **Nursing Foundation II** in the second semester (the two are averaged).

The **university theory exam is "Nursing Foundations (I & II)" at the end of the second semester**: one 3-hour, 75-mark paper (plus 25 internal marks), which can ask questions from **both** Nursing Foundation I and Nursing Foundation II. So everything in this pack will be examined — just one semester later, together with Nursing Foundation II. Do not let it go cold: keep revising it while you study Part II.

You must get at least 50% in theory and 50% in practical separately, and you must pass the mandatory First Aid module (pass mark 50%).

## The practice paper in this pack

Because there is no paper this semester, the mock test here is a **practice paper** set in the same pattern as the Nursing Foundations (I & II) university paper (INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3, 75-mark pattern), using only Part I topics. There is **no internal choice** — answer every question. Your university may print the paper differently; confirm with your university.

| Part | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 12 multiple-choice questions | 12 × 1 = 12 |
| Essay | 2 long (essay / situation-type) answers | 2 × 15 = 30 |
| Short | 5 short answers | 5 × 5 = 25 |
| Very short | 4 very short answers | 4 × 2 = 8 |
| **Total** | 3 hours | **75** |

There is also a **quick MCQ test** of 20 questions in 20 minutes for daily practice.

Suggested timing for the 3-hour paper: MCQs 10 minutes, each essay 40 minutes, each short answer 12–13 minutes, each very short answer 4 minutes, and 10 minutes to check.

## How the units are arranged

The INC syllabus has fourteen units, several of them very small. To keep each notes file a useful size, small related units are joined:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Theory hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Health, illness and health care delivery | I + II | 5 + 5 |
| Unit 2 History of nursing and nursing as a profession | III | 12 |
| Unit 3 Communication, nurse–patient relationship, documentation and reporting | IV + V | 8 + 4 |
| Unit 4 Vital signs | VI | 15 |
| Unit 5 Equipment and linen, infection control and a safe environment | VII + VIII + X | 3 + 10 + 5 |
| Unit 6 Comfort, rest and sleep, and pain | IX | 15 |
| Unit 7 Admission and discharge, mobility and immobility, patient education | XI + XII + XIII | 6 + 8 + 4 |
| Unit 8 First aid (including basic CPR) | XIV | 20 |

**What is not in this course**: personal hygiene of the patient (bed bath, oral care, hair care), the nursing process in detail, nutrition, elimination, oxygen therapy, and the full administration of medicines (routes, calculation of dosages) are taught in **Nursing Foundation II**. This pack covers the principles of safe medicine use only where Part I needs them — the "rights" of administration and the routes used for pain relief (Unit 6). No doses are given anywhere in this pack; doses are always as prescribed.

Procedures are written as **steps with the reason for each step** — learn the reasons, because examiners and OSCE assessors ask "why".

## Probability ratings

- **High** — a favourite; appears in most papers in some form. Learn the full answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but good for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from the syllabus hours, the competencies INC lists, and the usual style of nursing foundation papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | WHO definition and dimensions of health, Maslow's hierarchy, health–illness continuum, levels of prevention, levels of care |
| 2 | Florence Nightingale's contributions, history of nursing in India, functions and qualities of a nurse, nursing as a profession, code of ethics |
| 3 | Process and elements of communication, therapeutic and non-therapeutic techniques, phases of the nurse–patient relationship, purposes and guidelines of records, SBAR, incident report |
| 4 | Fever (stages, types, nursing care), tepid sponging, hot and cold applications, pulse sites and apical pulse, abnormal breathing patterns, BP measurement and errors |
| 5 | Chain of infection, HAI, medical vs surgical asepsis, hand washing steps, PPE, standard precautions, colour coding of biomedical waste, restraints, fall prevention, fire safety |
| 6 | Types of bed making (especially post-operative, cardiac, fracture), therapeutic positions, stages of sleep and promoting sleep, pain assessment and gate control theory |
| 7 | Admission and discharge procedures, LAMA, discharge planning, body mechanics, effects of immobility, crutch walking, care of a patient in a cast, principles of patient teaching |
| 8 | Principles of first aid, CPR, bleeding and shock, fractures and transport, burns (rule of nines), snake bite, poisoning, choking, triage |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Write procedures as numbered steps with a rationale**: "Count respiration with fingers still on the wrist — the patient does not change the breathing pattern." This is what "with rationale" questions want.
2. **Start every essay with a definition**, then a classification or list of types, then the main content in points, then **nursing responsibilities**, and finish with a line on documentation or health teaching.
3. **Use tables for comparisons**: fever vs hyperthermia, medical vs surgical asepsis, acute vs chronic pain, therapeutic vs non-therapeutic communication, types of beds, colour coding of waste.
4. **Draw simple diagrams**: the chain of infection, Maslow's pyramid, the communication process, the health–illness continuum, the rule of nines, pulse sites. Even a neat box diagram earns marks.
5. **Learn the numbers examiners like**: normal temperature, pulse, respiration, BP and SpO2 for adults and newborns; Fowler's angles; CPR rate, depth and ratio; WHO five moments; colour codes of the BMW Rules 2016; Florence Nightingale's dates; INC Act 1947.
6. **Situation-type essays** ("A 60-year-old patient is admitted with high fever…"): write assessment findings, two or three nursing problems, and the nursing care for each, with rationale.
7. **Very short answers (2 marks)**: a one-line definition plus one example or one fact.
8. **First aid answers**: always begin with safety and calling for help, and include a "do not" list.
9. MCQs come from small facts — read the "Remember" list of each notes file and the revision sheet the night before.
10. This course is also tested in the **practical exam and OSCE** — practise every procedure on a mannequin, saying the rationale aloud as you go.

# Last-night revision sheet: Nursing Foundation I

(Examined in the Nursing Foundations I & II paper at the end of the second semester.)

## Health and health care (Unit 1)

- **WHO 1948**: complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
- **Dimensions**: physical, mental, social, emotional, spiritual, intellectual, vocational, environmental.
- **Maslow**: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation.
- **Suchman's stages of illness**: symptom experience → sick role → medical care contact → dependent role → recovery.
- **Prevention**: primordial; primary (promotion + specific protection); secondary (early diagnosis, screening); tertiary (disability limitation, rehabilitation).
- **Care levels**: primary (SC, PHC) → secondary (CHC, district hospital) → tertiary (medical colleges). PHC 30,000 / CHC 1,20,000 (plains).

## History and profession (Unit 2)

- **Florence Nightingale**: 12 May 1820 – 13 August 1910; Kaiserswerth; Crimean War 1854 (Scutari); St Thomas' school 1860; *Notes on Nursing* 1859; statistics; 12 May = International Nurses Day.
- **India**: Charaka's four pillars; first school of nursing, Madras 1871; TNAI 1908; B.Sc Nursing 1946; INC Act 1947.
- **Functions**: independent, dependent, interdependent. **Metaparadigm**: person, environment, health, nursing.
- **Ethics**: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity, confidentiality, accountability.

## Communication and records (Unit 3)

- **Elements**: referent, sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context.
- **Therapeutic**: active listening, open questions, silence, clarifying, reflecting, restating, summarising.
- **Blocks**: false reassurance, advice, "why", changing the subject, judging, jargon.
- **Peplau phases**: (pre-interaction), orientation, working, termination.
- **SBAR**: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
- **Records**: date, time, signature; facts not opinions; single line through errors; no erasing; no blank lines; incident report kept out of the chart.
- **Systems**: source-oriented, POMR, SOAP(IE), PIE, focus (DAR), narrative, charting by exception, electronic.

## Vital signs (Unit 4)

| | Adult | Newborn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature (oral) | 36.5–37.5 °C | — |
| Pulse | 60–100/min | 120–160/min |
| Respiration | 12–20/min | 30–60/min |
| BP | below 120/80 mmHg | — |
| SpO2 | 95–100% | — |

- Axillary ≈ 0.5 °C lower, rectal ≈ 0.5 °C higher than oral. °F = °C × 9/5 + 32.
- **Fever** = set point raised; **hyperthermia** = set point normal, heat loss fails. Hyperpyrexia > 41 °C; hypothermia < 35 °C.
- **Stages**: onset (chills) → course (fastigium) → defervescence (crisis or lysis).
- **Types**: continuous (<1 °C swing), remittent (>1 °C, never normal), intermittent (back to normal — malaria), relapsing.
- **Tepid sponge**: lukewarm water, axillae and groins, slow strokes, stop if shivering, recheck after 30 minutes.
- **Heat**: vasodilation, relaxes. **Cold**: vasoconstriction, numbs, reduces swelling. About 20 minutes (rebound).
- **Pulse**: no thumb; full minute if irregular; apical = 5th ICS left MCL; **pulse deficit = apical − radial**.
- **Breathing patterns**: Cheyne–Stokes (cycles + apnoea), Kussmaul (deep, fast — DKA), Biot's (irregular + apnoea), orthopnoea (needs to sit up).
- **BP**: cuff bladder 40% width / 80% length; palpate first; inflate 30 mmHg above; deflate 2–3 mmHg/s; Korotkoff I = systolic, V = diastolic. Narrow cuff → high; wide → low; arm below heart → high.

## Infection control and safety (Unit 5)

- **Chain**: agent → reservoir → exit → transmission → entry → susceptible host.
- **Stages**: incubation → prodromal → illness → convalescence. **Inflammation**: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.
- **HAI**: ≥ 48 h after admission.
- **Medical asepsis** = clean; **surgical asepsis** = sterile (kills spores). Autoclave 121 °C, 15 lb/in², at least 15 min.
- **WHO 5 moments**; rub 20–30 s; wash 40–60 s.
- **PPE on**: gown → mask → goggles → gloves. **Off**: gloves → goggles → gown → mask → hand hygiene.
- **BMW Rules 2016**: Yellow — anatomical, soiled, chemical, expired medicines; Red — contaminated plastics (tubing, catheters, syringes without needles); White translucent — sharps; Blue — glass and metal implants. Untreated waste not beyond 48 h.
- **Fire**: RACE (Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate); PASS (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep).
- **Morse Fall Scale**: ≥ 45 high risk.
- **Restraints**: last resort; order + consent; tie to bed frame, quick-release knot, two fingers; check often; release about every 2 h; document.
- **Rubber goods**: cold water, dry, powder, store flat. Never shake linen.

## Comfort, sleep, pain (Unit 6)

- **Beds**: closed (awaiting admission), open (ambulant), occupied, post-operative (fan-fold, vomit protection, emergency tray), cardiac (sitting up, cardiac table), fracture (fracture boards, cradle), amputation (divided covers, tourniquet ready).
- **Positions**: Fowler's low 15–30°, semi 30–45°, high 60–90°; orthopnoeic; Sims' (left side, right knee up — enema); dorsal recumbent; lithotomy; knee–chest; Trendelenburg (head low).
- **Sleep**: N1, N2, N3 (deep), REM; ~90-minute cycles; melatonin; insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, parasomnias.
- **Pain**: whatever the patient says it is (McCaffery); PQRST; NRS 0–10, VAS, Wong–Baker FACES, FLACC; Pasero sedation scale for opioids.
- **Gate control theory**: Melzack and Wall 1965. **WHO ladder**: non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid ± adjuvants.
- **PCA**: lockout interval; only the patient presses. **TENS**: not over the front of the neck or with a pacemaker.
- **Rights**: right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation (+ reason, response, refusal). Doses only as prescribed.

## Admission, mobility, teaching (Unit 7)

- **Admission**: welcome, ID band, orient, baseline vital signs and weight, history, valuables signed, inform doctor, record.
- **Discharge planning starts at admission**: METHOD (Medications, Environment, Treatment, Health teaching, Outpatient follow-up, Diet).
- **LAMA**: inform doctor, explain risks, signed form. **Abscond**: search, inform, record.
- **Body mechanics**: wide base, low centre of gravity, load close, legs not back, pivot not twist, push not lift.
- **Immobility**: pressure ulcers, contractures, osteoporosis, DVT, orthostatic hypotension, hypostatic pneumonia, constipation, UTI/stones, depression.
- Wheelchair at 45° on the strong side, brakes on; walk on the weak side; cane in the strong hand; crutches — weight on hands, not axillae; up with the good, down with the bad.
- **Cast**: palms, elevate, 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis); unrelieved pain = report (compartment syndrome).
- **Teaching**: cognitive, affective, psychomotor; return demonstration; teach-back.

## First aid (Unit 8)

- **Aims**: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery. **DRSABCD**. Call **112 / 108**.
- **Bleeding**: direct pressure ≥ 10 min, elevate, add pads; tourniquet only for life-threatening limb bleeding (note time). Nosebleed: lean forward, pinch.
- **Shock**: lay flat, raise legs, warm, nothing by mouth.
- **Fracture**: immobilise joint above and below. **Sprain**: RICE. **Dislocation**: don't reduce.
- **Choking**: adult 5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts; infant back blows + chest thrusts.
- **CPR (adult)**: 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, full recoil, 30:2, AED early. Child 5 cm, infant 4 cm; two rescuers 15:2.
- **Unconscious**: AVPU, GCS 3–15; recovery position if breathing. **FAST** for stroke. Fits: don't restrain, nothing in the mouth.
- **Burns**: cool running water ~20 min; no ice/butter/toothpaste; don't burst blisters. Rule of nines: head 9, arm 9 each, front 18, back 18, leg 18 each, perineum 1. Palm ≈ 1%.
- **Poisoning**: don't induce vomiting; keep the container. **Snake bite** (Big Four: cobra, krait, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper): immobilise, no cut/suck/tight tourniquet, hospital. **Dog bite**: soap + running water ~15 min, anti-rabies vaccine.
- **Frostbite**: warm gently, never rub. **Heat stroke**: cool fast, ambulance.
- **Triage**: red immediate, yellow delayed, green minor, black dead/expectant. NDMA under the DM Act 2005.

1. Definition (WHO, 1948): health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. Positive and wide, but 'complete' makes it an ideal.
2. Dimensions (with a nursing example each): physical (normal body function — vital signs, mobility); mental (clear thinking, coping); social (relationships, role in family); emotional (expressing feelings); spiritual (meaning, faith); intellectual (learning); vocational (work satisfaction); environmental (safe water, housing). The dimensions affect one another.
3. Factors influencing health: internal — genetics, age, sex, developmental stage, beliefs, emotions; lifestyle — diet, exercise, sleep, smoking, alcohol, stress; environmental — water, sanitation, housing, pollution, occupation; socio-economic — income, education, employment, gender; cultural — food habits, health beliefs; health services — availability, cost, distance, quality.
4. Health–illness continuum: health and illness are two ends of a line; a person moves along it. Travis: illness side (premature death, disability, symptoms, signs) — neutral point — wellness side (awareness, education, growth, high-level wellness). Treatment brings a person to the neutral point; education and growth move them towards wellness.
5. Dunn's high-level wellness grid: health axis × environment axis gives four quadrants (high-level wellness in favourable environment, emergent wellness in unfavourable, protected poor health, poor health in unfavourable).
6. Diagram: a horizontal arrow with illness and wellness ends and a neutral point.
7. Nursing implications: assess where the patient is, care for all dimensions (holistic), reduce modifiable risk factors through teaching, help people with chronic illness achieve the highest wellness possible.
questions.question: Define health. Explain the dimensions of health and the factors influencing health. Add a note on the health–illness continuum.

questions.answer:
1. Abraham Maslow arranged human needs in five levels; lower needs must be at least partly met before higher ones motivate behaviour.
2. Diagram: a pyramid — base physiological, then safety and security, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualisation at the top.
3. Physiological needs: oxygen, fluids, food, elimination, temperature, sleep, rest, freedom from pain, sexual needs. Nursing: airway, oxygen, IV fluids, feeding, bedpan, rest, pain relief.
4. Safety and security: physical safety (falls, infection, burns) and psychological security (freedom from fear). Nursing: side rails, call bell, hand hygiene, explaining procedures, orientation to ward.
5. Love and belonging: affection, acceptance, family. Nursing: involve family, flexible visiting, warmth, listening.
6. Esteem: self-respect, recognition, independence. Nursing: address by name, privacy, consent, encourage self-care, praise progress.
7. Self-actualisation: reaching one's potential. Nursing: help set personal goals, rehabilitation, education for return to work.
8. Priority setting: life-threatening physiological needs first (ABC — airway, breathing, circulation), then other physiological needs, then safety, then the higher needs. Example: a breathless patient is positioned and given oxygen before health teaching.
9. Limitations: the order may change with culture or person; a person can have several needs at once; not based on patients. Still the most used priority framework.
10. Conclusion: it ensures holistic care and logical priorities.
questions.question: Explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs with a diagram. How does a nurse use it to set priorities of patient care?

questions.answer:
1. Prevention: actions that stop disease starting, catch it early or limit its effects.
2. Primordial: prevent risk factors arising in a population (healthy lifestyle teaching to children).
3. Primary: before disease — health promotion (health education, nutrition, sanitation, exercise) and specific protection (immunisation, iodised salt, helmets, chemoprophylaxis).
4. Secondary: early diagnosis and prompt treatment — screening for BP, diabetes, cancers; case finding.
5. Tertiary: disability limitation and rehabilitation — physiotherapy after stroke, artificial limbs, vocational training.
6. Levels of care: primary (first contact, near home — sub-centres/Health and Wellness Centres, PHCs); secondary (specialist care on referral — CHCs, district hospitals); tertiary (super-specialty, teaching, research — medical colleges, AIIMS). Norms (plains): SC 5,000; PHC 30,000; CHC 1,20,000 (3,000/20,000/80,000 in hilly and tribal areas). A referral system links levels.
7. Agencies: hospitals, clinics/dispensaries, hospices (palliative end-of-life care), rehabilitation centres, extended care facilities/nursing homes, home health care, day-care centres.
8. Health team: doctor (diagnosis, treatment), nurse (24-hour care, assessment, treatment, teaching, co-ordination), pharmacist, dietitian, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, medical social worker, laboratory and radiology staff, counsellor, ASHA/health workers, support staff.
9. Nurse's place: co-ordinator of the team because she is with the patient round the clock.
questions.question: Describe the levels of prevention and the levels of health care in India. List the types of health care agencies and the members of the health care team with their roles.

questions.answer:
1. Primordial: stop risk factors appearing — teaching healthy diet and exercise in schools.
2. Primary: health promotion (education, nutrition, sanitation) and specific protection (immunisation, iodised salt, helmet use) — before disease.
3. Secondary: early diagnosis and prompt treatment — BP and diabetes screening, Pap smear, breast self-examination.
4. Tertiary: disability limitation and rehabilitation — physiotherapy after stroke, artificial limbs.
5. Diagram: health → risk factors → early disease → advanced disease → disability, with each level placed under its stage.
questions.question: Explain the levels of prevention with examples.

questions.answer:
Illness behaviour = how people notice symptoms, interpret them and seek help (Suchman).
1. Symptom experience: notices something wrong; feels concern; decides if serious.
2. Assumption of the sick role: accepts being ill; seeks lay advice; may stay off work.
3. Medical care contact: seeks professional diagnosis and treatment.
4. Dependent patient role: relies on health workers, follows treatment.
5. Recovery and rehabilitation: gives up the sick role, resumes duties.
Influenced by age, culture, knowledge, cost, distance, past experience. Nurse respects beliefs and corrects misconceptions.
questions.question: Describe the stages of illness behaviour.

questions.answer:
Patient: changed body image, loss of independence and roles, fear and anxiety, pain and disturbed sleep, loss of income, low self-esteem, loneliness in hospital.
Family: role changes, financial burden, emotional stress, disturbed routine, care-giving load and fatigue, changed relationships, children feeling neglected.
Nursing role: explain the illness, involve the family in care plans, teach care-giving skills, refer to social worker or support groups, watch for carer strain.
questions.question: Write about the impact of illness on the patient and family.

questions.answer:
1. Types: by ownership — government, private, voluntary/trust; by function — general, specialty, teaching, research; by length of stay — short and long stay; by size; by system — modern medicine, AYUSH.
2. Organisation: governing body → medical superintendent → medical services, nursing service (chief nursing officer → deputy/assistant nursing superintendents → ward sisters → staff nurses → students and support staff), diagnostic, support (pharmacy, dietary, laundry, CSSD) and administrative departments.
3. Functions: patient care (diagnosis, treatment, nursing, rehabilitation), prevention and health promotion, education of health workers, research.

questions.answer: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO, 1948).

questions.answer: A factor that increases the chance of developing an illness without causing it by itself. Examples: smoking (lung cancer, heart disease); family history of diabetes.

questions.answer: A health care service giving comfort (palliative) care to people in the last stage of a terminal illness, controlling pain and symptoms and supporting the family, rather than trying to cure.

questions.answer:
1. Born 12 May 1820 in Florence, Italy, to a wealthy English family; well educated; felt called to serve.
2. Trained at the Kaiserswerth deaconess institute (Pastor Fliedner), Germany (1851); superintendent of a hospital for gentlewomen in London (1853).
3. Crimean War 1854: went to Scutari with 38 nurses; found filth, no linen, poor food, high mortality; organised cleaning, laundry, kitchens, sanitation and records; death rates fell; 'Lady with the Lamp'.
4. Nightingale Fund → Nightingale Training School at St Thomas' Hospital, London, 1860 — first organised secular nursing school.
5. Writings: Notes on Nursing (1859), Notes on Hospitals; many reports.
6. Honours: first woman to receive the Order of Merit (1907); died 13 August 1910; International Nurses Day on 12 May.
Contributions:
7. Nursing education — planned course, selection, nurse teachers, residence.
8. Environmental approach — fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, clean water, drainage (basis of her theory).
9. Use of statistics — collected death data, polar area ('coxcomb') diagrams to persuade government.
10. Hospital planning — pavilion wards, cross-ventilation, bed spacing.
11. Made nursing a respectable career for women with discipline and ethics.
12. Observation and recording of patients' condition.
13. Army and public health reform, including sanitation of the army in India.
14. Conclusion: founder of modern nursing; her principles remain the base of infection control and patient-centred care.
questions.question: Write a brief life history of Florence Nightingale and describe her contributions to nursing.

questions.answer:
1. Definitions (paraphrase): Nightingale — putting the patient in the best condition for nature to act; Henderson — helping the person, sick or well, perform activities for health, recovery or peaceful death that they would do unaided with strength, will or knowledge, and helping them become independent; ICN — autonomous and collaborative care of people of all ages, sick or well, including health promotion, illness prevention, care of the ill, disabled and dying, advocacy and research.
2. Nature/characteristics: art and science; holistic; caring and helping; for sick and well; uses the nursing process; dynamic; 24-hour service; based on ethics.
3. Scope: hospital (wards, ICU, OT, emergency), community health, education, administration, specialised and advanced practice (nurse practitioner, midwifery, critical care, mental health), occupational health, military nursing, research, private/home care, international.
4. Functions: independent (positioning, hygiene, comfort, teaching, observation); dependent (giving prescribed medicines and treatments); interdependent (collaborative planning with the team).
5. Roles: caregiver, communicator, teacher, counsellor, advocate, manager, co-ordinator, change agent, researcher, leader.
6. Qualities — personal: good health, neatness, honesty, patience, kindness, emotional stability, punctuality, tact; professional: knowledge, skill, accuracy, observation, judgement, responsibility, confidentiality, eagerness to learn; social: respect for all, teamwork, courtesy, empathy.
7. Conclusion: these qualities and functions make nursing a caring profession.
questions.question: Define nursing. Explain the nature, scope and functions of nursing, and the qualities of a nurse.

questions.answer:
1. Profession: an occupation needing long specialised education, with its own body of knowledge, service orientation and code of ethics.
2. Criteria met by nursing: body of knowledge (theories, research); university education (B.Sc, M.Sc, PhD); service to society; code of ethics (ICN, INC); professional organisation (INC, state councils, TNAI); autonomy (independent functions); career ladder and continuing education; registration with the state council.
3. Values: beliefs about what is good and important that guide behaviour. Professional values: human dignity, altruism, autonomy, integrity, social justice, caring, accountability. Importance: guide decisions and dilemmas, build trust, consistent care; values clarification prevents bias.
4. Ethical principles: autonomy (consent), beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (no harm — patient identification), justice (fair care), veracity (truth), fidelity (keep promises), confidentiality, accountability.
5. Code of ethics: written principles a profession agrees to follow. ICN Code (first adopted 1953) — nurses and people, practice, profession, co-workers/global health. INC Code of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct guide Indian nurses.
6. Main duties: respect life and dignity without discrimination; confidentiality; competence and updating knowledge; accountability; protect patients from unsafe practice; respect colleagues; good personal conduct; contribute to the profession.
7. Professional conduct: punctuality, uniform, courtesy, honest records, no misuse of drugs or gifts. Misconduct (negligence, falsifying records, breach of confidentiality, abuse) leads to council action including removal from the register.
questions.question: Explain nursing as a profession. Discuss values, ethical principles and the code of ethics and professional conduct for nurses.

questions.answer:
1. Ancient: Charaka Samhita — four pillars (physician, medicine, attendant, patient) and qualities of an attendant; Sushruta on surgical care; Ashoka's hospitals.
2. Muslim period: Unani hospitals.
3. 1664: East India Company hospital at Fort St George, Madras.
4. 19th century: midwifery training in Madras; first school of nursing at Government General Hospital, Madras, 1871; mission hospitals trained Indian nurses; military nursing services.
5. 1908: TNAI formed. 1926: Madras Registration Council.
6. 1946: Bhore Committee; B.Sc Nursing at College of Nursing Delhi and CMC Vellore.
7. 1947: INC Act — Indian Nursing Council for uniform standards; later M.Sc, PhD, nurse practitioner programmes; revised curriculum 2021.
questions.question: Write the history of nursing in India.

questions.answer:
1. Specialised knowledge — nursing theories, research, nursing process.
2. University-level education — B.Sc, M.Sc, PhD.
3. Service to society — care of sick and promotion of health.
4. Code of ethics — ICN and INC codes.
5. Professional organisation — INC, state councils, TNAI.
6. Autonomy — independent nursing functions.
7. Registration/licensing — state nursing councils.
8. Lifelong commitment and career ladder — continuing education, promotions.
questions.question: List the criteria of a profession and explain how nursing fulfils them.

questions.answer: Autonomy — right to decide (informed consent). Beneficence — do good (timely care). Non-maleficence — do no harm (checking identity before procedures). Justice — fair care regardless of status. Veracity — truthfulness. Fidelity — keeping promises. Confidentiality — protect information. Accountability — answer for one's actions (reporting own error).
questions.question: Explain the ethical principles in nursing with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Independent: decided and done on nursing knowledge — positioning, hygiene, comfort measures, health teaching, observation, bed making.
2. Dependent: done on a doctor's written order — giving medicines, IV fluids, special diets.
3. Interdependent (collaborative): with other team members — discharge planning with doctor, physiotherapist and social worker.
4. Roles within these: caregiver, teacher, counsellor, advocate, manager, co-ordinator, researcher.
questions.question: Describe the functions of a nurse.

questions.answer: Florence Nightingale. International Nurses Day is celebrated on 12 May, her birthday.

questions.answer: Physician, medicine (drugs), attendant (nurse) and patient.

questions.answer: Actions a nurse performs on the written order of a doctor, such as giving prescribed medicines, IV fluids or a special diet.
