# Unit 2: History of nursing and nursing as a profession

INC Unit III (12 hours): history of nursing in the world and in India, the contributions of Florence Nightingale, the meaning, scope and functions of nursing, nursing as a profession, values, and the code of ethics and professional conduct for nurses.

## 2.1 Why study the history of nursing?

History shows how nursing grew from untrained, religious or family care into a profession with its own education, council and ethics. It explains why we follow certain practices (clean hands, fresh air, record keeping), gives pride in the profession, and shows how today's problems were solved before.

## 2.2 History of nursing in the world

| Period | Main features |
| --- | --- |
| Primitive times | Illness blamed on evil spirits; care given by mothers and the family; the medicine man used charms and herbs |
| Ancient civilisations | Egypt: embalming, knowledge of herbs. Greece: Hippocrates (father of medicine) taught observation and natural causes of disease. Rome: military hospitals |
| Early Christian era | Care of the sick seen as a religious duty. Deaconesses (Phoebe is often named as the first visiting nurse). Fabiola, a Roman woman, set up a free hospital in Rome |
| Middle Ages | Religious orders and monasteries ran hospitals. Military nursing orders (Knights Hospitallers) cared for pilgrims and soldiers during the Crusades |
| "Dark period" of nursing (about 1500–1850) | After the Reformation many monasteries closed. Nursing was done by poorly paid, untrained and often uneducated women. Hospitals were dirty and overcrowded. Charles Dickens's character Sairey Gamp became a symbol of this careless nurse |
| Reform period | Pastor Theodor Fliedner started a deaconess institute at Kaiserswerth, Germany (1836), training women in nursing; Florence Nightingale trained there. Modern nursing began with Nightingale's school in 1860 |
| 20th century onwards | Nursing councils and registration, the International Council of Nurses (ICN, founded 1899), university degrees in nursing, specialisation, nursing research and nurse practitioners |

## 2.3 Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): founder of modern nursing

**Life in brief**

- Born on **12 May 1820** in Florence, Italy, to a wealthy English family; she was named after the city. She was well educated in languages, mathematics and philosophy.
- Felt a "call" to serve. Against her family's wishes she trained at **Kaiserswerth** (1851) and later became superintendent of a hospital for gentlewomen in London (1853).
- **Crimean War (1854)**: she went with 38 nurses to the British military hospital at **Scutari**. She found filth, no clean linen, poor food and very high death rates. She organised cleaning, laundry, kitchens, sanitation and records. Death rates fell sharply. She walked the wards at night with a lamp — "**the Lady with the Lamp**".
- After the war the public raised the **Nightingale Fund**, which she used to open the **Nightingale Training School for Nurses at St Thomas' Hospital, London, in 1860** — the first secular, organised school of nursing.
- Wrote **Notes on Nursing** (1859) and **Notes on Hospitals**, and many reports.
- She took great interest in the **health of the army and people of India**, and her reports helped improve sanitation in Indian cantonments.
- First woman to receive the **Order of Merit (1907)**. Died on **13 August 1910**.
- **International Nurses Day** is celebrated on her birthday, **12 May**.

**Her contributions**

1. **Nursing education** — a planned course, a residence for students, selection of good-character candidates, and nurse teachers.
2. **Environment and hygiene** — fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, clean water and drainage. Her environmental theory still guides patient care.
3. **Statistics** — she collected and analysed death rates and showed them in diagrams (the polar area or "coxcomb" diagram) to persuade the government. She is seen as a pioneer of using data in health care.
4. **Hospital planning** — pavilion wards with cross-ventilation and good spacing of beds.
5. **Nursing as a respectable career for women**, with dignity, discipline and ethics.
6. **Observation and records** — she taught nurses to observe patients carefully and record what they saw.
7. **Public health and the army** — reforms in military health and sanitation.

The **Nightingale Pledge**, recited by students at the lamp-lighting ceremony, was written in her honour (in 1893) by a committee in the USA; she did not write it herself.

## 2.4 History of nursing in India

| Time | Event |
| --- | --- |
| Ancient India | The **Charaka Samhita** describes the four pillars of treatment: physician, medicine, attendant (nurse) and patient, and the qualities of a good attendant — knowledge, skill, devotion to the patient and cleanliness. **Sushruta** described surgery and the care of surgical patients. Emperor **Ashoka** (3rd century BC) is said to have built hospitals for people and animals |
| Muslim period | Unani medicine; hospitals (shifakhanas) in large cities |
| 1664 | The East India Company opened a hospital for soldiers at **Fort St George, Madras** — the first of the British-style hospitals |
| 19th century | Training of midwives began in Madras; the **first school of nursing** was started at the **Government General Hospital, Madras, in 1871**. Mission hospitals in many places trained Indian women as nurses. Military nursing services for the British army in India were organised in the late 1800s |
| 1908 | The **Trained Nurses' Association of India (TNAI)** was formed |
| 1926 | The **Madras Registration Council** — the first state body to register nurses |
| 1946 | The Bhore Committee (Health Survey and Development Committee) recommended better nursing education and more nurses. **B.Sc Nursing** began at the College of Nursing, Delhi, and Christian Medical College, Vellore |
| 1947 | The **Indian Nursing Council Act** was passed, creating the **Indian Nursing Council (INC)** to bring uniform standards of nursing education across the country |
| After independence | Post-basic B.Sc, M.Sc and PhD programmes; state nursing councils in every state; nurse practitioner programmes; INC revised the B.Sc curriculum (Regulations 2020, notified 2021) |

**Main nursing bodies in India**

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Indian Nursing Council (INC) | Statutory body; lays down syllabus and standards, recognises institutions |
| State Nursing and Midwifery Councils | Register nurses and midwives to practise in the state; conduct some exams |
| TNAI | Professional association; welfare, conferences, journal (*The Nursing Journal of India*) |
| Military Nursing Service (MNS) | Nurses in the armed forces |

## 2.5 Nursing: definitions and concepts

**Nurse**: a person who has completed a recognised nursing programme and is registered to practise, who cares for people who are sick or well.

**Nursing — well-known views** (in our words)

- **Florence Nightingale**: nursing is putting the patient in the best possible condition so that nature can do its healing work.
- **Virginia Henderson**: the nurse helps a person, sick or well, to carry out the activities that lead to health, recovery or a peaceful death, which the person would do alone if they had the strength, will or knowledge — and to make them independent as soon as possible.
- **International Council of Nurses**: nursing covers independent and collaborative care of people of all ages, families, groups and communities, sick or well, in all settings. It includes promoting health, preventing illness and caring for the ill, disabled and dying, plus advocacy, research and shaping health policy.

**Central concepts of nursing (the metaparadigm)**

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Person | The receiver of care — an individual, family or community, with physical, mental, social and spiritual needs |
| Environment | Internal and external surroundings that affect the person |
| Health | The person's position on the health–illness continuum |
| Nursing | The actions the nurse takes with and for the person |

**Philosophy of nursing**: belief in the worth and dignity of every person, the right of everyone to good health care without discrimination, care of the whole person, and the nurse's duty to keep learning.

**Objectives of nursing**: promote health, prevent illness, restore health, help people cope with disability, and support a peaceful death.

## 2.6 Characteristics, nature and scope of nursing

**Characteristics / nature**

- It is both an **art** (caring, compassion, communication) and a **science** (knowledge from anatomy, physiology, microbiology, psychology).
- It is **holistic** — caring for body, mind and spirit.
- It is **helping and caring**, and it is for people **sick and well**.
- It uses the **nursing process** — a systematic, problem-solving method.
- It is **dynamic**, changing with new knowledge and technology.
- It is a **24-hour service**.

**Scope of nursing**

| Area | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Hospital nursing | Wards, ICU, operation theatre, emergency, dialysis |
| Community health nursing | Sub-centres, PHCs, home visits, school health, national programmes |
| Nursing education | Teachers, principals, clinical instructors |
| Nursing administration | Ward in-charge, nursing superintendent, chief nursing officer |
| Specialised practice | Critical care, oncology, cardiac, mental health, paediatric, midwifery, nurse practitioner |
| Industrial / occupational health | Factories, industries |
| Military nursing | Armed forces |
| Research | Nursing studies to improve care |
| Private and independent practice | Home care, consultation |
| International nursing | WHO, abroad |

## 2.7 Functions of a nurse

| Function | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Independent | Actions the nurse decides and does on her own knowledge | Positioning, bed making, health teaching, comfort measures, hygiene, observation |
| Dependent | Actions done on the written order of a doctor | Giving prescribed medicines, IV fluids, special diets |
| Interdependent (collaborative) | Done jointly with other team members | Planning discharge with the doctor, physiotherapist and social worker |

**Roles of the nurse**: caregiver, communicator, teacher/educator, counsellor, advocate (speaking up for the patient's rights), manager, co-ordinator, change agent, researcher, leader, rehabilitator, comforter.

## 2.8 Qualities of a nurse

- **Personal**: good health, neat appearance, honesty, patience, kindness, emotional stability, sense of humour, punctuality, tact.
- **Professional**: sound knowledge, skill, accuracy, keen observation, good judgement, responsibility, ability to keep confidences, interest in learning.
- **Social and ethical**: respect for all people without discrimination, team spirit, courtesy, loyalty, sympathy and empathy (understanding the patient's feelings without being overwhelmed).

## 2.9 Categories of nursing personnel in India

| By education | By position (typical hospital) |
| --- | --- |
| Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) | Nursing officer / staff nurse |
| General Nursing and Midwifery (GNM) | Senior nursing officer / ward sister |
| B.Sc Nursing; Post-basic B.Sc Nursing | Assistant / Deputy Nursing Superintendent |
| M.Sc Nursing; Nurse Practitioner programmes | Nursing Superintendent / Chief Nursing Officer |
| M.Phil / PhD in Nursing | In education: tutor, lecturer, professor, principal |

Support workers (nursing assistants, ward attendants) help but are not registered nurses.

## 2.10 Nursing as a profession

A **profession** is an occupation that needs long, special education, has its own body of knowledge, serves society and is controlled by its own code of ethics.

**Criteria of a profession and how nursing meets them**

| Criterion | Nursing |
| --- | --- |
| Specialised body of knowledge | Nursing theories, research, nursing process |
| Education in a university | B.Sc, M.Sc, PhD in nursing |
| Service to society | Care of the sick and promotion of health |
| Code of ethics | ICN and INC codes |
| Professional organisation | INC, state councils, TNAI |
| Autonomy | Independent nursing functions, nurse practitioners |
| Lifelong commitment and career ladder | Continuing education, promotion |
| Licensing / registration | Registration with the state nursing council |

## 2.11 Values

**Values** are the beliefs a person holds about what is right, good and important; they guide behaviour. **Professional values** for nurses include:

- **Human dignity** — respect for every person's worth and uniqueness.
- **Altruism** — concern for the welfare of others.
- **Autonomy** — respecting the patient's right to decide.
- **Integrity** — honesty and acting by the code.
- **Social justice** — fair care for all regardless of caste, religion, money or gender.
- **Caring, accountability and excellence.**

**Why values matter**: they guide decisions in difficult situations, build public trust, help in ethical dilemmas, and make care consistent. A nurse should be aware of her own values so they do not bias care (values clarification).

## 2.12 Ethics, code of ethics and professional conduct

**Ethics** is the study of right and wrong conduct. **Ethical principles** in nursing:

| Principle | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomy | Respect the patient's right to make decisions | Taking informed consent |
| Beneficence | Do good | Giving timely care |
| Non-maleficence | Do no harm | Checking a patient's identity before a procedure |
| Justice | Be fair | Giving care by need, not by status |
| Veracity | Tell the truth | Not giving false hope |
| Fidelity | Keep promises | Returning when you said you would |
| Confidentiality | Keep information private | Not discussing a patient in the canteen |
| Accountability | Answer for your actions | Reporting your own error |

**Code of ethics**: a written set of principles that a profession agrees to follow. The **ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses** (first adopted in 1953 and revised since) groups the nurse's duties under nurses and patients/people, nurses and practice, nurses and the profession, and nurses and global health/co-workers. In India the **INC Code of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct for Nurses** set out the same ideas for Indian practice; read the current version on the INC website.

Main points of these codes (in our words):

1. Respect the life, dignity and rights of every person, without discrimination.
2. Keep patient information confidential and share it only for care or as the law requires.
3. Practise within your competence and keep your knowledge up to date.
4. Take responsibility and be accountable for your own actions.
5. Protect patients from unsafe or unethical practice and report it.
6. Work co-operatively and respectfully with colleagues.
7. Keep high standards of personal conduct that bring credit to the profession.
8. Take part in improving health care and the profession.

**Professional conduct** is behaving according to these standards: punctuality, proper uniform, polite speech, no acceptance of gifts that may influence care, no misuse of drugs or records, honesty in documentation, and respect for colleagues. **Professional misconduct** (negligence, falsifying records, breaching confidentiality, abusing a patient) can lead to disciplinary action by the nursing council, including removal from the register.

## Remember

- Florence Nightingale: born 12 May 1820, Crimean War 1854 (Scutari, 38 nurses), school at St Thomas' Hospital 1860, *Notes on Nursing* 1859, died 1910; International Nurses Day = 12 May.
- Kaiserswerth (Pastor Fliedner) trained Nightingale.
- India: first school of nursing at Government General Hospital, Madras, 1871; TNAI 1908; B.Sc Nursing 1946 (Delhi and Vellore); INC Act 1947.
- Charaka Samhita: physician, medicine, attendant, patient.
- Functions: independent, dependent, interdependent.
- Metaparadigm: person, environment, health, nursing.
- Ethical principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity, confidentiality.
- Profession: special knowledge, university education, service, ethics, organisation, autonomy, registration.

# Unit 3: Communication, nurse–patient relationship, documentation and reporting

INC Unit IV (8 hours theory + 3 skill lab): communication and the nurse–patient relationship. INC Unit V (4 hours theory + 2 skill lab): documentation and reporting. They are joined because both are about passing information accurately — by talking and by writing.

## 3.1 Communication: meaning

**Communication** is the exchange of information, thoughts and feelings between people through words, signs, writing and behaviour, so that both understand the same meaning. In nursing it is the tool for assessment, teaching, comfort and teamwork.

## 3.2 Levels of communication

| Level | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intrapersonal | Talking to oneself, inner thoughts | "I can do this injection safely" |
| Interpersonal | Between two people | Nurse talking with a patient |
| Transpersonal | Communication with a higher power or the spiritual self | Prayer, meditation |
| Small group | Among a few people | Ward meeting, health team conference |
| Public | One person to a large audience | Health talk in a village |

## 3.3 Elements and process of communication

```text
          ┌─────────── Feedback ◄────────────┐
          ▼                                   │
     SENDER ──encodes──► MESSAGE ──channel──► RECEIVER ──decodes
     (nurse)            (words, gestures)     (patient)
                       ↑
             CONTEXT / environment (noise, privacy, culture)
```

| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Referent (stimulus) | What starts the communication — a pain, a need, a question |
| Sender (encoder) | Person who forms and sends the message |
| Message | The information, verbal or non-verbal |
| Channel | The route: speech, sight, touch, writing, phone, email |
| Receiver (decoder) | Person who receives and interprets the message |
| Feedback | The receiver's response, showing whether the message was understood |
| Environment / context | Setting in which it happens — time, place, privacy, noise |

The process is a cycle: the sender forms an idea, puts it in words or signs, sends it; the receiver takes it in, interprets it and responds with feedback.

## 3.4 Types and modes of communication

| Type | Features | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verbal (spoken or written) | Uses words; should be simple, clear, brief, well-timed, suited to the listener, credible | Explaining a procedure; written instructions |
| Non-verbal | Body language; often more honest than words | Facial expression, eye contact, posture, gestures, touch, tone of voice, silence, appearance, personal space |
| Formal | Through official channels | Shift report, written order |
| Informal | Casual, personal | Chat at the bedside |
| One-way / two-way | Only sender speaks / both speak and give feedback | A notice board / a counselling session |

**Personal space** (distance zones): intimate (touching to about 45 cm — used in procedures, so explain first), personal (about 45 cm–1.2 m — most nurse–patient talks), social (about 1.2–3.6 m), public (beyond 3.6 m).

## 3.5 Factors influencing communication

- **Perception** — each person sees things through their own experience.
- **Values and beliefs**, **culture and language**.
- **Emotions** — anxiety, anger and pain block listening.
- **Developmental stage** — children and the elderly need adapted language.
- **Gender and social roles**.
- **Knowledge level** — avoid medical jargon.
- **Physical condition** — hearing loss, speech problems, sedation, pain.
- **Environment** — noise, lack of privacy, interruptions.
- **Space and territory**, and **relationship** between the people.

## 3.6 Therapeutic communication techniques

**Therapeutic communication** is purposeful, patient-centred communication that helps the patient express feelings, understand the illness and cope.

| Technique | What the nurse does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active listening | Gives full attention, maintains eye contact, nods | (Sits down, faces the patient) |
| Broad opening | Lets the patient choose the topic | "What would you like to talk about?" |
| Open-ended question | Invites a full answer, not yes/no | "How have you been feeling since the surgery?" |
| Silence | Gives time to think and feel | (Pauses quietly) |
| Restating / paraphrasing | Repeats the main idea in other words | "You are worried about going home alone." |
| Clarifying | Asks to make the meaning clear | "Do you mean the pain is worse at night?" |
| Reflecting | Returns the feeling to the patient | "You sound frightened." |
| Focusing | Keeps the talk on one important point | "Let's talk more about your breathlessness." |
| Sharing observations | States what the nurse notices | "You seem tense today." |
| Giving information | Provides facts the patient needs | "The test takes about ten minutes." |
| Offering self | Shows willingness to be with the patient | "I'll sit with you for a while." |
| Summarising | Pulls together the main points | "So, you've told me three things…" |
| Therapeutic touch | Holding a hand, when culturally acceptable | |

## 3.7 Barriers / non-therapeutic communication

| Block | Example | Why it harms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| False reassurance | "Don't worry, everything will be fine." | Brushes feelings aside; may be untrue |
| Giving advice | "If I were you, I would…" | Takes away the patient's decision |
| Approval / disapproval | "That's bad, you shouldn't think that." | Judges; patient stops sharing |
| Asking "why" | "Why did you stop your tablets?" | Feels like an accusation |
| Changing the subject | Talking about the weather when the patient mentions death | Shows the nurse is uncomfortable |
| Stereotyped comments | "Everyone feels that way." | Feels like a cliché |
| Defensive reply | "The doctors here are very good." | Protects the staff, not the patient |
| Too many / closed questions | "Did you sleep? Eat? Pass urine?" | Turns talk into an interrogation |
| Jargon, talking too fast | "Your Hb is low; you need a PRBC transfusion." | Not understood |

Other barriers: noise, pain, language difference, hearing loss, anxiety, hurry, lack of privacy, cultural taboos.

## 3.8 Professional communication

Communication with doctors, colleagues and other staff should be **clear, concise, factual, timely and respectful**, and kept confidential. A common structured method for passing urgent information is **SBAR** (or ISBAR):

| Step | Content |
| --- | --- |
| (I) Identify | Yourself, the unit and the patient |
| S — Situation | What is happening now |
| B — Background | Diagnosis, relevant history, treatment |
| A — Assessment | What you found (vital signs, observations) and what you think |
| R — Recommendation | What you need or suggest; confirm the plan |

Repeat back any verbal or telephone order, write it down, and get it signed as early as possible according to hospital policy.

## 3.9 The helping relationship (nurse–patient relationship)

A **helping (therapeutic) relationship** is a planned, goal-directed, professional relationship in which the nurse helps the patient meet health needs. It is centred on the patient, has a time limit, and ends when goals are met.

**Purposes**: to build trust, help the patient express feelings, understand the illness, solve problems, cope, and become independent.

**Phases** (based on Hildegard Peplau's work)

| Phase | What happens | Nurse's tasks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-interaction | Before meeting the patient | Read the records, examine own feelings, plan the first meeting |
| Orientation (introductory) | First meetings; getting to know each other | Introduce self, explain role, agree on goals and time, begin to build trust, maintain confidentiality |
| Working (identification and exploitation) | Main work of the relationship | Help the patient explore feelings, give care and information, encourage self-care, solve problems |
| Termination (resolution) | Ending | Prepare the patient for discharge or transfer in advance, review progress, deal with feelings about separation |

Qualities that help: **trust, empathy** (understanding the patient's feelings), **genuineness**, **respect**, **warmth**, **active listening** and **confidentiality**. Sympathy (feeling sorry for someone) is different from empathy and is less helpful.

## 3.10 Communicating with patients, families and the team

- **Patients**: introduce yourself, call them by preferred name, explain before you touch, check understanding (ask them to repeat — the "teach-back" method), allow questions.
- **Families**: keep them informed within confidentiality rules, involve them in care, listen to their worries.
- **Team**: accurate handover, use SBAR, respect roles, resolve disagreements privately.

## 3.11 Communicating with vulnerable groups

| Group | Helpful approach |
| --- | --- |
| Children | Speak at their eye level, simple words, play and pictures, involve parents, be honest about pain |
| Women | Privacy, a female attendant during examinations, sensitivity in reproductive or abuse issues |
| Hearing impaired | Face the person, good light, speak slowly (do not shout), use writing or sign language, hearing aid on |
| Visually impaired | Announce yourself, describe surroundings, guide by offering your arm |
| Speech impaired | Yes/no questions, picture boards, allow time |
| Mentally challenged | Short sentences, patience, repetition, involve carers |
| Elderly | Allow more time, check hearing and vision, speak clearly, show respect, do not talk down |
| Different language | Use a trained interpreter, not a child of the family |

## 3.12 Documentation: purposes of records and reports

A **record** is a permanent written (or electronic) account of the patient's care. A **report** is an oral or written exchange of information about patients among health workers.

**Purposes of records**

1. **Communication** among team members.
2. **Planning and continuity of care** across shifts.
3. **Legal document** — evidence of what care was given; may be used in court.
4. **Quality review and audit**.
5. **Education** of students.
6. **Research and statistics**.
7. **Billing, insurance and reimbursement**.
8. **Health statistics** for planning services.

## 3.13 Confidentiality

Information in records belongs to the patient and must be shared only with people directly involved in care, or as required by law. The nurse must not leave charts open, discuss patients in public places, share passwords or post anything about patients on social media. Medical records are handed over only through the medical records department with proper authorisation. Breaking confidentiality is a breach of ethics and may lead to legal action.

## 3.14 Types of client records / common forms

Admission sheet (identification data), history and physical examination record, doctor's order sheet, **nurses' notes** (progress notes), **graphic (TPR) chart**, intake–output chart, medication administration record (MAR), Kardex (a quick-reference card of current care), care plan, investigation reports, consent forms, operation notes, anaesthesia record, transfer form, discharge summary, incident report (kept separately).

## 3.15 Methods / systems of documentation

| System | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Source-oriented record | Each discipline writes in its own section (doctor's notes, nurses' notes, lab) — traditional, but information is scattered |
| Problem-oriented medical record (POMR) | Organised around the patient's problems: database, problem list, plan, progress notes |
| SOAP / SOAPIE / SOAPIER | Subjective data, Objective data, Assessment, Plan (+ Intervention, Evaluation, Revision) |
| PIE | Problem, Intervention, Evaluation |
| Focus charting (DAR) | Data, Action, Response for each focus (a concern or event) |
| Narrative | Story-like notes in time order — easy to write, hard to search |
| Charting by exception (CBE) | Only abnormal findings written; normal ones checked against set standards |
| Computerised / electronic health records | Fast, legible, accessible; need password protection |
| Flow sheets and checklists | Repeated observations (vital signs, intake–output) in tables |

## 3.16 Guidelines for documentation

Good records are **accurate, complete, concise, current, factual, legible, organised and confidential**.

**Do's**

- Write in blue or black ink (as per hospital policy) or enter electronically.
- Write the date and time of each entry, and sign with name and designation.
- Record facts: what you saw, heard, measured and did, and the patient's response. Quote the patient's own words when useful.
- Record as soon as possible after care; never before it is done.
- Use only approved abbreviations and correct spelling.
- If you make a mistake, draw a single line through it, write "mistaken entry" or "error", initial and date it, and write the correct entry.
- Write a late entry clearly labelled as "late entry" with the actual time.
- Record refusals of treatment and informing the doctor.

**Don'ts**

- Do not erase, use correction fluid, overwrite or tear pages.
- Do not leave blank lines (draw a line through empty space).
- Do not write opinions or labels ("patient is rude", "drunk"); describe behaviour instead.
- Do not chart for someone else or let someone chart for you.
- Do not write "error" without correcting it, or blame colleagues in the notes.
- Do not mention an incident report in the patient's record (record only the facts of what happened and the care given).

**Legal guidelines**: the record is a legal document; what is not recorded may be treated as not done. Keep records safely for the period the hospital and law require.

## 3.17 Reporting

| Report | Purpose and content |
| --- | --- |
| Change-of-shift (handover) report | Given by the outgoing nurse to the incoming nurse, oral (at the bedside or station), written or recorded. Includes identity, diagnosis, condition and changes, vital signs, treatments due, investigations, pending tasks, patient concerns. Bedside handover allows the patient to take part |
| Transfer report | When a patient moves to another unit or hospital: identity, diagnosis, condition, vital signs, medicines last given, allergies, special equipment, family informed, belongings, records sent |
| Incident (occurrence / variance) report | Written report of any unexpected event that harmed or could have harmed a patient, visitor or staff member — fall, medication error, needle-stick injury, equipment failure. Written promptly and factually; used to improve safety, not to punish. Kept separately from the patient's record |
| Telephone report / order | Read back, record time, name of caller, and get signed |

## Remember

- Elements: referent, sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context.
- Levels: intrapersonal, interpersonal, transpersonal, small group, public.
- Therapeutic techniques: listening, open questions, silence, clarifying, reflecting, summarising.
- Non-therapeutic: false reassurance, advice, "why" questions, changing the subject, judging.
- Peplau phases: (pre-interaction), orientation, working, termination.
- SBAR = Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
- Records are legal documents: date, time, sign; single line through errors; no erasing; no blank spaces.
- Documentation systems: source-oriented, POMR, SOAP(IE), PIE, focus (DAR), narrative, charting by exception, electronic.
- Incident report: factual, prompt, kept out of the patient's chart.

# Unit 4: Vital signs

INC Unit VI (15 hours theory + 20 hours skill lab): body temperature, pulse, respiration, oxygen saturation and blood pressure — their physiology, how to measure them, their alterations, hot and cold applications, and how to record them. This is the largest unit of the course and the most practical one; it is also a favourite for OSCE.

## 4.1 Vital signs: meaning and guidelines

**Vital signs** (cardinal signs) are measurements that show how well the body's essential functions are working: **temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure**. **Oxygen saturation (SpO2)** and **pain** are often called the fifth and sixth vital signs.

**When to take them**: on admission (baseline), as ordered or by ward routine, before and after surgery or an invasive procedure, before and after giving some medicines that affect the heart or breathing, when the patient's condition changes or they say they feel unwell, before and after nursing interventions such as ambulation, and during blood transfusion.

**General guidelines**

1. Know the patient's usual (baseline) values and medical history.
2. Use equipment that is clean, working and of the right size.
3. Control or note factors that change the readings: exercise, eating, smoking, crying, pain, room temperature.
4. Take them in a calm setting with the patient resting and comfortable.
5. Explain what you will do; ask permission.
6. Use a systematic method and measure accurately; repeat if a value seems wrong.
7. Interpret the values against normal ranges and the patient's baseline.
8. Record promptly and report abnormal values or sudden changes at once.

## 4.2 Body temperature: physiology and regulation

**Body temperature** is the balance between heat produced and heat lost. **Core temperature** (deep tissues: abdomen, chest, brain) stays fairly constant; **surface temperature** (skin) varies with the surroundings.

**Heat production**: basal metabolism, muscle activity and shivering, thyroxine and adrenaline (raise metabolism), digestion, fever.

**Heat loss**

| Method | Meaning | Nursing use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Radiation | Heat moves from the body surface to cooler objects without contact | Removing heavy blankets in fever |
| Conduction | Heat moves to a cooler object in direct contact | Ice pack, cooling blanket |
| Convection | Heat carried away by moving air | Fan in fever |
| Evaporation | Water (sweat) turns to vapour and takes heat | Tepid sponging |

**Regulation**: the **hypothalamus** acts as the thermostat. Receptors in the skin and core send information to it. When the body is hot, the **anterior hypothalamus** starts heat loss (sweating, vasodilation of skin vessels). When cold, the **posterior hypothalamus** conserves and produces heat (vasoconstriction, shivering, goose flesh, more metabolism).

**Normal values**

| Site | Normal range (adult, approximate) |
| --- | --- |
| Oral | 36.5–37.5 °C (average 37 °C = 98.6 °F) |
| Axillary | About 0.5 °C lower than oral |
| Rectal | About 0.5 °C higher than oral (closest to core) |
| Tympanic | Close to core temperature |

Conversion: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32; °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9.

**Factors affecting body temperature**: age (newborns regulate poorly; the elderly run lower and may not show fever), **diurnal variation** (lowest early in the morning, highest late afternoon and evening), exercise, hormones (temperature rises slightly after ovulation and in pregnancy), stress and emotions, environment, food and fluids, smoking, illness and medicines.

## 4.3 Assessment of body temperature: sites, equipment and technique

| Site | Advantages | Avoid in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral (under the tongue, in the posterior sublingual pocket) | Easy, comfortable | Infants and young children, unconscious, confused or restless patients, mouth breathers, after oral surgery, seizures, breathlessness; wait 15–30 minutes after hot or cold food, drinks or smoking |
| Axillary | Safe, non-invasive; good for children and unconscious patients | Gives lower readings; needs a dry axilla and correct placement |
| Tympanic (ear canal) | Quick, close to core | Ear infection, ear wax, ear surgery |
| Rectal | Most accurate of these sites | Diarrhoea, rectal surgery or disease, heart patients (vagal stimulation), newborns (risk of perforation); used only when other sites are unsuitable |
| Temporal artery (forehead scanner) | Quick, non-invasive | Sweaty forehead, head covering |

**Equipment**: digital (electronic) thermometer, tympanic thermometer, temporal artery thermometer, disposable chemical-dot thermometer. Glass mercury thermometers are being phased out because mercury is toxic; if one breaks, follow the hospital's mercury spill procedure.

**Procedure: oral temperature with a digital thermometer**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Check the order/routine; wash hands; gather equipment | Prevents infection; saves time |
| 2. Identify the patient; explain the procedure | Right patient; gains co-operation |
| 3. Ask whether the patient has had hot/cold food or drink or smoked in the last 15–30 minutes | These change mouth temperature and give a false reading |
| 4. Put on a clean probe cover; switch on the thermometer | Prevents cross-infection |
| 5. Place the tip under the tongue in the posterior sublingual pocket, to one side | This pocket lies near large blood vessels and reflects core temperature |
| 6. Ask the patient to close the lips (not the teeth) and breathe through the nose | Keeps the probe in place; prevents cooling by air; teeth may break the probe |
| 7. Leave in place until the device signals | Gives an accurate reading |
| 8. Remove, read, discard the probe cover in the correct bin | Prevents spread of micro-organisms |
| 9. Clean the thermometer as per policy; wash hands | Infection control |
| 10. Record on the graphic chart and report abnormal values | Communication and continuity of care |

**Axillary temperature**: dry the axilla (moisture cools the skin), place the tip in the centre of the axilla, lower the arm and fold it across the chest to keep the probe in contact, and wait for the signal. A glass thermometer needs longer in the axilla than in the mouth; follow your procedure manual.

**Tympanic temperature**: gently pull the pinna **up and back** in adults (**down and back** in children under three) to straighten the ear canal; fit the probe snugly so it points at the eardrum; read.

## 4.4 Alterations in body temperature

| Alteration | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Fever (pyrexia)** | Body temperature above normal because pyrogens (from infection, tissue injury, inflammation) **raise the hypothalamic set point** |
| **Hyperthermia** | Body temperature above normal while the set point is unchanged — the body cannot lose heat fast enough (heat stroke, some drug reactions) |
| Hyperpyrexia | Very high fever, above about 41 °C (105.8 °F); dangerous to the brain |
| **Heat cramps** | Painful muscle spasms after heavy sweating and salt loss in heat |
| **Heat exhaustion** | Weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, heavy sweating, cool moist skin, fast weak pulse; caused by fluid and salt loss; temperature normal or moderately raised |
| **Heat stroke** | Failure of heat regulation: very high temperature (above about 40 °C), hot dry skin (sweating may stop), confusion, seizures, unconsciousness — an emergency |
| **Hypothermia** | Core temperature below 35 °C: shivering (which stops as it worsens), pale cold skin, slow pulse and breathing, confusion. Mild 32–35 °C, moderate 28–32 °C, severe below 28 °C |

## 4.5 Fever: definition, causes, stages and types

**Grades of fever** (texts differ slightly): low grade about 37.5–38 °C; moderate 38–39 °C; high 39–41 °C; hyperpyrexia above 41 °C.

**Causes**: infections (bacterial, viral, malarial), tissue injury and surgery, inflammation, dehydration, some cancers, blood transfusion reactions, drug reactions, brain injury affecting the hypothalamus.

**Stages of fever**

| Stage | What happens | Signs | Nursing care |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Onset (invasion, chill phase) | Set point rises; body produces and conserves heat to reach it | Chills, shivering, cold pale skin, goose flesh, fast pulse | Warm blanket, warm drinks, record temperature |
| 2. Course (fastigium, plateau) | Temperature stays at the new high level | Hot flushed skin, thirst, headache, malaise, dry mouth, loss of appetite, restlessness; delirium if high | Remove extra covers, cooling measures, fluids, mouth care, rest |
| 3. Termination (defervescence) | Set point returns to normal; body loses heat | Sweating, flushed skin | Dry and change clothes and linen, fluids, rest |

Defervescence may be by **crisis** (a sudden fall within hours) or by **lysis** (a gradual fall over days).

**Types of fever**

| Type | Pattern | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Continuous (sustained) | Stays above normal; daily variation less than 1 °C | Typhoid, lobar pneumonia |
| Remittent | Stays above normal but varies by more than 1 °C during the day | Many bacterial infections |
| Intermittent | Present for some hours each day, then returns to normal | Malaria, septicaemia |
| Quotidian, tertian, quartan | Intermittent fever recurring every day, every third day (48 h), every fourth day (72 h) | Types of malaria |
| Relapsing | Days of fever alternate with days of normal temperature | Relapsing fever (Borrelia), Hodgkin's (Pel–Ebstein) |
| Septic (hectic) | Wide swings between very high and normal, with chills and sweats | Abscess, septicaemia |

**Nursing management of a patient with fever**

1. Monitor temperature (every 4 hours, or more often if high), pulse and respiration; record on the graphic chart.
2. Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room; light clothing and bed covers.
3. Plenty of oral fluids unless restricted; record intake and output (fluid is lost in sweat and breathing).
4. Light, nourishing, easily digested diet in small amounts.
5. Cooling measures: tepid sponging, cold compress on the forehead, ice cap (see 4.6).
6. Mouth care (dry mouth, coated tongue), skin care, change of damp linen.
7. Give antipyretics and other medicines as prescribed and check the response.
8. Safety: side rails if delirious; watch children for febrile convulsions.
9. Observe for chills, sweating, dehydration, delirium; report hyperpyrexia at once.

## 4.6 Hot and cold applications

**Effects**

| Heat | Cold |
| --- | --- |
| Vasodilation — more blood flow | Vasoconstriction — less blood flow |
| Relaxes muscles, relieves stiffness and spasm | Numbs nerve endings, reduces pain |
| Speeds healing and suppuration (localises infection) | Reduces swelling and bleeding |
| Increases metabolism and capillary permeability | Slows metabolism and inflammation |
| | Lowers body temperature (tepid sponge) |

**Types**

| | Dry | Moist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heat | Hot water bag, electric heating pad, aquathermia pad, infrared lamp | Hot compress, fomentation, sitz bath, soaks, steam inhalation |
| Cold | Ice cap / ice bag, ice collar, chemical cold pack | Cold compress, tepid sponge, cold soaks |

Moist heat penetrates deeper but burns more easily; dry heat lasts longer but dries the skin.

**Contraindications**

| For heat | For cold |
| --- | --- |
| First hours after an injury (increases swelling and bleeding) | Impaired circulation (Raynaud's disease, peripheral vascular disease) |
| Acute inflammation such as appendicitis (may cause rupture) | Open wounds (delays healing) |
| Active bleeding | Shivering, very young or very old |
| Non-inflammatory oedema | Cold allergy (hypersensitivity) |
| Impaired sensation or confusion; unconscious patients | Impaired sensation |
| Over a malignancy, testes, abdomen in pregnancy | |

**Rebound phenomenon**: the greatest effect is reached in about 20–30 minutes; if heat or cold is left on much longer, the body reacts in the opposite way (for example vessels constrict again under prolonged heat). So applications are usually limited to about 20 minutes and repeated after a rest, as ordered.

**Safety**: check the temperature of water with a bath thermometer (do not rely on touch); for a hot water bag many texts give about 46–52 °C for an adult and lower for children, older adults and unconscious patients — follow your hospital procedure; always cover the bag; check the skin often; never place a bag under a patient; ask the patient to report burning or numbness.

**Procedure: tepid sponging** (to reduce a high temperature by evaporation and conduction)

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Check order; take and record the temperature, pulse and respiration | Baseline for evaluation |
| 2. Explain; give privacy; close windows to avoid draught | Co-operation; dignity; prevents chilling |
| 3. Prepare a basin of lukewarm water a few degrees below body temperature (texts give about 27–34 °C), checked with a bath thermometer, sponge cloths, towels, mackintosh, ice cap | Water slightly cooler than the body removes heat without causing shivering |
| 4. Remove the patient's clothes, cover with a sheet; place mackintosh and towel under the part | Exposes skin for cooling while keeping dignity; protects the bed |
| 5. Put a cold compress or ice cap on the forehead | Cools the head and prevents headache |
| 6. Place wet cloths in the axillae and groins | Large blood vessels lie close to the skin there, so heat loss is faster |
| 7. Sponge face, arms, chest, abdomen, legs and back with long, slow strokes towards the heart, changing cloths often; leave the skin moist | Slow strokes and moisture allow evaporation, which cools; strokes towards the heart aid venous return |
| 8. Continue for about 20–30 minutes; stop if the patient shivers, looks pale or blue, or the pulse becomes weak | Shivering produces heat and defeats the purpose; signs of chilling must be acted on |
| 9. Pat dry, dress in light clothes, make comfortable | Comfort; prevents chilling |
| 10. Recheck the temperature about 30 minutes later; record and report | Evaluates the effect |

**Ice cap**: fill about two-thirds with small pieces of ice (large lumps leave gaps and do not fit the part), expel the air, close, check for leaks, dry, cover with a cloth; apply for about 20 minutes; check the skin; refill as needed.

**Cold compress**: wring out a cloth soaked in cold water, apply to the part (forehead, a sprain), change every few minutes as it warms.

## 4.7 Pulse

**Definition**: the throb of an artery felt over a bony surface, caused by the wave of blood forced into the aorta when the left ventricle contracts.

**Physiology and regulation**: the heartbeat starts in the **sinoatrial (SA) node** (the pacemaker). Each beat sends a stroke volume into the arteries; cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. The **sympathetic** nerves and adrenaline speed the heart; the **vagus nerve** (parasympathetic) slows it.

**Characteristics of the pulse**

| Characteristic | Normal and abnormal |
| --- | --- |
| Rate (beats per minute) | Adult 60–100. Above 100 = **tachycardia**; below 60 = **bradycardia** (athletes may normally be slower) |
| Rhythm | Regular intervals. Irregular = **dysrhythmia/arrhythmia**. Sinus arrhythmia (rate rises with inspiration) is normal in children |
| Volume (strength) | Graded 0 absent, 1+ weak/thready, 2+ normal, 3+ full/bounding |
| Tension | Resistance of the vessel wall; hard in arteriosclerosis |
| Equality | Pulses on both sides should be equal |

**Normal pulse rates by age (approximate)**: newborn 120–160; infant 100–160; toddler 90–150; school-age child 70–110; adolescent and adult 60–100.

**Factors affecting pulse**: age, sex (women slightly faster), exercise, fever (the rate rises as the temperature rises), emotions and pain, haemorrhage and shock (fast, weak), position (faster on standing), medicines, hypoxia, raised intracranial pressure (slow).

**Pulse sites**

```text
Temporal (in front of the ear)
Carotid (side of neck — never press both at once)
Apical (5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line)
Brachial (inner elbow — infants, BP)
Radial (thumb side of wrist — most common)
Femoral (groin)
Popliteal (back of knee)
Posterior tibial (behind the inner ankle)
Dorsalis pedis (top of the foot)
```

**Procedure: radial pulse**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Wash hands; explain; let the patient rest 5–10 minutes | Activity raises the rate |
| 2. Patient sitting or lying, forearm resting across the chest or at the side, wrist slightly flexed | Relaxes the tendons over the artery so it is easier to feel |
| 3. Place the tips of the first two or three fingers on the radial artery | Fingertips are sensitive; **the thumb is not used** because it has its own pulse |
| 4. Press gently until the pulse is felt | Too much pressure blocks the artery |
| 5. Count for 30 seconds and double it if regular; count a **full minute** if irregular, first assessment, or the patient is very ill | Accuracy |
| 6. Note rhythm, volume and tension | Complete assessment |
| 7. Record and report abnormalities | Communication |

**Apical pulse**: listen with a stethoscope at the 5th intercostal space in the left midclavicular line for a full minute. Used for infants and young children, irregular pulses, heart disease, and before giving some heart medicines.

**Apical–radial pulse and pulse deficit**: two nurses count at the same time for one full minute using one watch — one at the apex, one at the radial artery. **Pulse deficit = apical rate − radial rate.** A deficit means some beats are too weak to reach the wrist (for example in atrial fibrillation).

**Other alterations**: thready (weak, fast, in shock), bounding (strong, in fever or anxiety), pulsus paradoxus (weaker during inspiration), pulsus alternans (alternate strong and weak beats, in heart failure), water-hammer or collapsing pulse (aortic regurgitation).

## 4.8 Respiration

**Definition**: the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide. It has three parts: **ventilation** (moving air in and out of the lungs), **diffusion** (gas exchange between alveoli and blood) and **perfusion** (blood flow through the lungs).

**Regulation**: respiratory centres in the **medulla oblongata and pons**. The main stimulus is a rise in carbon dioxide (detected by central chemoreceptors); low oxygen stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.

**Mechanics of breathing**: in **inspiration** (active) the diaphragm contracts and moves down, the external intercostals lift the ribs, the chest enlarges, pressure falls and air flows in. **Expiration** is normally **passive**: the muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil.

**Characteristics**: rate, depth, rhythm, effort and sounds.

**Normal rates (approximate)**: newborn 30–60; infant 30–50; young child 20–30; adolescent and adult 12–20 breaths per minute.

**Factors affecting respiration**: age, exercise, fever, pain, anxiety, altitude, smoking, anaemia, position, medicines (opioids slow breathing), disease of the lungs and brain.

**Procedure: counting respiration**

1. Count immediately after the pulse **while keeping your fingers on the wrist**, so the patient does not know breathing is being watched (people change their breathing when they know).
2. One breath = one rise and fall of the chest.
3. Count for 30 seconds and double if regular; count a full minute if irregular, in infants, or if abnormal.
4. Note depth, rhythm, effort, use of accessory muscles, colour of skin and lips, and any noise.
5. Record and report.

**Alterations in respiration**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Eupnoea | Normal, quiet breathing |
| Tachypnoea | Rapid breathing (fever, anxiety, pneumonia) |
| Bradypnoea | Slow breathing (opioids, raised intracranial pressure) |
| Apnoea | No breathing |
| Hyperventilation | Fast, deep breathing; blows off CO2 |
| Hypoventilation | Slow, shallow breathing; CO2 builds up |
| Dyspnoea | Difficult, laboured breathing |
| Orthopnoea | Can breathe comfortably only when sitting up (heart failure) |
| Cheyne–Stokes | Cycles of breathing that grow deeper then shallower, followed by apnoea (heart failure, brain damage, near death) |
| Kussmaul | Deep, fast, regular breathing (metabolic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis) |
| Biot's | Irregular breaths of varying depth with sudden apnoea (brain injury, meningitis) |
| Stridor | Harsh, high-pitched sound on inspiration (upper airway blockage) |
| Wheeze | Whistling sound, mainly on expiration (asthma) |
| Stertor | Snoring sound (unconscious patient, secretions) |

## 4.9 Arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2)

**SpO2** is the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen, measured without a needle by a **pulse oximeter**, which shines red and infrared light through a finger, toe or earlobe. Normal is about **95–100%**; values below about 90% show significant hypoxaemia and must be reported at once (follow the patient's prescribed target).

**Procedure**: choose a site with good circulation; remove nail polish or artificial nails; warm cold hands; attach the probe so the light source and sensor face each other; keep the hand still; wait for a steady reading and a good pulse wave; compare the displayed pulse with the patient's pulse; record. For continuous monitoring, move a finger probe every few hours to prevent pressure injury.

**Sources of error**: movement, cold or poorly perfused fingers, nail polish, bright external light, severe anaemia, and carbon monoxide poisoning (gives a falsely normal reading).

## 4.10 Blood pressure

**Definitions**

- **Blood pressure**: the force exerted by blood against the walls of the arteries.
- **Systolic pressure**: the highest pressure, during ventricular contraction.
- **Diastolic pressure**: the lowest pressure, when the ventricles relax.
- **Pulse pressure** = systolic − diastolic (normally about 40 mmHg).
- **Mean arterial pressure** ≈ diastolic + one-third of the pulse pressure.

**Physiology and regulation**: BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance. It also depends on blood volume, blood viscosity and the elasticity of the arteries. It is controlled by **baroreceptors** in the carotid sinus and aortic arch (quick nervous control), the **renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system** and antidiuretic hormone (long-term control through salt and water), and the kidneys.

**Normal values (adult)**: ideally below 120/80 mmHg. **Hypertension** is generally diagnosed when readings are 140/90 mmHg or more on repeated measurements; Indian and international guidelines grade the levels slightly differently. **Hypotension** is usually below 90/60 mmHg. **Orthostatic (postural) hypotension**: a fall of 20 mmHg or more systolic (or 10 mmHg or more diastolic) within a few minutes of standing, with dizziness.

**Factors affecting BP**: age (rises with age), sex, time of day (lowest early morning), exercise, stress, pain, obesity, race and heredity, posture, salt intake, smoking, alcohol, medicines, disease (kidney, heart), blood loss.

**Sites**: brachial artery (usual), radial (forearm), popliteal (thigh — cuff over the thigh, when arms cannot be used), posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis (lower leg).

**Equipment**: sphygmomanometer (aneroid dial, digital/automatic; mercury instruments are being phased out), cuff of correct size, stethoscope. The **bladder of the cuff should be about 40% of the arm's circumference wide and about 80% of it long**.

**Korotkoff sounds**: the sounds heard as the cuff is deflated. The **first clear tapping sound (phase I) = systolic**; the **point where sounds disappear (phase V) = diastolic** in adults. A silent period between them in some hypertensive patients is the **auscultatory gap**; missing it gives a falsely low systolic reading.

**Procedure: brachial blood pressure (two-step method)**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Patient rested for about 5 minutes; no caffeine, smoking or exercise in the previous 30 minutes; bladder empty | These raise BP temporarily |
| 2. Seated with back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed, arm bared and supported at heart level, palm up | Arm below heart level gives a falsely high reading; above gives falsely low |
| 3. Avoid an arm with an IV line, AV fistula, injury, or on the side of a mastectomy | Prevents harm and false readings |
| 4. Choose the correct cuff; wrap it snugly 2–3 cm above the elbow crease with the bladder centre over the brachial artery | Too small a cuff gives a falsely high reading; too large gives falsely low; correct position compresses the artery evenly |
| 5. Palpate the radial artery, inflate until the pulse disappears, and note this reading; deflate | Estimates systolic pressure and avoids missing an auscultatory gap |
| 6. Wait about 30 seconds | Lets blood flow return to normal |
| 7. Place the stethoscope lightly over the brachial artery (not under the cuff) | Pressing hard distorts the sounds |
| 8. Inflate to about 30 mmHg above the palpated reading | Ensures the artery is fully closed |
| 9. Release the valve so the needle falls about 2–3 mmHg per second | Too fast deflation gives an inaccurate (often low systolic) reading |
| 10. Note the first sound (systolic) and the point where sounds disappear (diastolic) | Korotkoff phases I and V |
| 11. Deflate fully; remove the cuff; wait 1–2 minutes before repeating | Venous congestion gives false readings |
| 12. Record (for example 118/76 mmHg, right arm, sitting); report abnormal values | Communication; site and position affect the value |

**Common errors in BP assessment**

| Error | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Cuff too narrow or too loose | Falsely high |
| Cuff too wide | Falsely low |
| Arm below heart level | Falsely high |
| Arm above heart level | Falsely low |
| Deflating too quickly | Systolic falsely low, diastolic falsely high |
| Deflating too slowly | Venous congestion; diastolic falsely high |
| Repeating too soon | Falsely high systolic |
| Missing the auscultatory gap | Systolic falsely low |
| Eye not level with the dial or mercury | Reading error |
| Patient talking, anxious or after exercise | Falsely high |

**Alterations**: hypertension (headache, nosebleed, but often no symptoms — "silent"), hypotension (dizziness, fainting, pale cold skin in shock), orthostatic hypotension (after bed rest, in the elderly, with some medicines — help such patients to sit, then stand slowly).

## 4.11 Documenting vital signs and care of equipment

- Record on the **graphic (TPR) chart** at the correct time column; plot temperature and pulse as dots joined by lines in the colours your hospital uses (commonly blue for temperature and red for pulse); write respiration, BP and SpO2 in the spaces provided.
- Note the site and method (oral, axillary; right arm, lying) when relevant.
- Write abnormal findings and the action taken in the nurses' notes, and report them.
- Use the hospital's early-warning score if one is in use, and call for help as the score requires.

**Care of equipment**: clean digital thermometers with an alcohol swab and use probe covers; clean the stethoscope earpieces and diaphragm with alcohol between patients; keep BP cuffs clean and fully deflated, store the tubing without kinks and send instruments for regular checking (calibration); wipe pulse oximeter probes between patients.

## Remember

- Normal adult: temperature 36.5–37.5 °C (oral), pulse 60–100/min, respiration 12–20/min, BP below 120/80 mmHg, SpO2 95–100%.
- Fever = raised set point (pyrogens); hyperthermia = normal set point but heat loss fails.
- Stages of fever: onset (chill), course (fastigium), defervescence (crisis or lysis).
- Continuous (<1 °C variation, typhoid), remittent (>1 °C, never normal), intermittent (returns to normal, malaria).
- Tepid sponge: lukewarm water, axillae and groins, long strokes, stop if shivering, recheck after about 30 minutes.
- Heat dilates and relaxes; cold constricts, numbs and reduces swelling; about 20 minutes (rebound).
- Never take a pulse with your thumb. Apical pulse: 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line, full minute.
- Pulse deficit = apical − radial (two nurses, one watch).
- Count respiration with fingers still on the wrist.
- Cuff bladder 40% × 80% of arm circumference; narrow cuff → falsely high; deflate 2–3 mmHg per second.
- Korotkoff I = systolic, V = diastolic; the auscultatory gap is why we palpate first.
