# Unit 5: Equipment and linen, infection control and a safe environment

INC Unit VII (3 hours): equipment and linen. INC Unit VIII (10 hours theory + 3 skill lab): infection control in the clinical setting and biomedical waste management. INC Unit X (5 hours theory + 3 skill lab): promoting safety in the health care environment. They are joined because all three are about keeping the patient's surroundings clean, safe and well supplied.

## 5.1 Hospital equipment and linen: types

Equipment is either **disposable** (single use, then discarded — syringes, gloves, catheters, probe covers) or **reusable** (cleaned, disinfected or sterilised and used again — instruments, bedpans, BP cuffs).

| Type | Examples | Care |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linen | Sheets, draw sheets, pillow covers, blankets, towels, gowns, patient clothes, screens | Count and send soiled linen in the correct bag; infected linen in a separate labelled bag; never shake linen (spreads dust and micro-organisms); store clean linen in a closed, dry cupboard |
| Rubber goods | Mackintosh, hot water bags, ice caps, air cushions, tubing, gloves | Wash in cold or lukewarm water (heat damages rubber), dry both sides, powder lightly, store flat or hanging without folds, away from heat, oil and sharp objects; hot water bags stored with a little air inside so the sides do not stick |
| Glassware | Measuring jars, specimen bottles, glass syringes (now rare) | Rinse in cold water first (hot water sets protein), wash, dry, store safely; broken glass into the blue box |
| Metal articles | Instruments, kidney trays, bowls, bedpans | Rinse in cold water, clean with detergent and brush, dry well to prevent rusting; lubricate hinges; sterilise as required; never mix sharp instruments with heavy articles |
| Enamel ware | Bowls, trays | Avoid knocking (chips cause rust) |
| Plastics | Bowls, jugs, bedpans, tubing | Wash with warm (not boiling) water and detergent; many cannot be autoclaved |
| Furniture | Beds, lockers, over-bed tables, chairs, stretchers, wheelchairs | Damp dust daily, check wheels and brakes, report repairs |

## 5.2 Indent, inventory and maintenance

- **Indent**: a written request for supplies from the store or pharmacy, usually on a fixed day; it lists the item, quantity in stock and quantity needed, and is signed by the in-charge.
- **Inventory**: a record of all equipment and linen in the ward, checked regularly (stock book); missing or broken items are reported; old items are written off (condemned) by the proper procedure.
- **Maintenance**: **preventive** (regular cleaning, checking and servicing to avoid breakdown) and **corrective** (repair after breakdown). Faulty equipment is labelled "not for use" and sent for repair.
- Rules: use equipment only for its purpose, return borrowed items, keep a fixed place for each article, teach staff to handle items correctly.

## 5.3 Nature of infection

**Infection** is the entry and multiplication of micro-organisms in the body that causes harm. **Colonisation** is the presence of micro-organisms without harm. A **pathogen** causes disease; **virulence** is its power to do so.

## 5.4 Chain of infection

Infection spreads only when all six links are present. Breaking **any one link** stops it.

```text
   1. Infectious agent ──► 2. Reservoir ──► 3. Portal of exit
          ▲                                          │
          │                                          ▼
   6. Susceptible host ◄── 5. Portal of entry ◄── 4. Mode of transmission
```

| Link | Examples | How the nurse breaks it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infectious agent | Bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites | Prompt diagnosis and treatment, disinfection, sterilisation |
| Reservoir | People, animals, food, water, soil, equipment, wet surfaces | Hygiene, clean environment, dry equipment, change dressings |
| Portal of exit | Respiratory secretions, blood, urine, faeces, wound drainage | Cover mouth when coughing, careful handling of body fluids, cover wounds |
| Mode of transmission | Contact (direct, indirect), droplet, airborne, vehicle (food, water, blood), vector (mosquito) | **Hand hygiene**, PPE, isolation, safe food and water |
| Portal of entry | Broken skin, mucous membranes, respiratory, urinary, GI tracts, catheters | Aseptic technique, catheter care, skin care |
| Susceptible host | Very young, elderly, malnourished, immunosuppressed, diabetic, after surgery | Nutrition, immunisation, rest, treat underlying disease |

## 5.5 Types and stages of infection

**Types**: local (in one area, a boil) and systemic (spreads through the body, septicaemia); acute and chronic; primary and secondary (a new infection on top of the first); exogenous (from outside) and endogenous (from the patient's own flora); communicable; **iatrogenic** (caused by a treatment or procedure); **opportunistic** (caused by organisms that are normally harmless, in a weak host).

**Stages of infection**

| Stage | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Incubation period | From entry of the organism to the first symptoms; the organism multiplies |
| Prodromal stage | Vague, general symptoms (tiredness, mild fever); the person is often infectious |
| Illness (full stage) | Specific signs and symptoms of the disease |
| Convalescence | Symptoms subside and the person recovers |

## 5.6 Factors increasing susceptibility to infection

Extremes of age, poor nutrition, stress and fatigue, chronic diseases (diabetes, cancer, kidney failure), immunosuppression (steroids, chemotherapy, HIV), broken skin (wounds, burns), invasive devices (catheters, IV lines, ventilators), long hospital stay, inadequate immunisation, smoking.

## 5.7 Body defences against infection

1. **First line (non-specific barriers)**: intact skin, mucous membranes, cilia, tears, saliva and lysozyme, stomach acid, normal flora, flushing by urine, coughing and sneezing.
2. **Second line — the inflammatory response**: when tissue is injured, blood vessels dilate and become leaky; white cells (neutrophils, macrophages) move in and engulf organisms (phagocytosis). Five signs: **redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function**. Stages: vascular and cellular response → inflammatory exudate (serous, purulent, sanguineous) → tissue repair. Fever is also part of the defence.
3. **Third line — the immune response**: specific defence by lymphocytes. **Humoral immunity** (B cells make antibodies) and **cell-mediated immunity** (T cells). Immunity may be natural or acquired, active (infection, vaccine) or passive (maternal antibodies, ready-made antibodies).

## 5.8 Health care associated (nosocomial) infection

A **health care associated infection (HAI)** is an infection a patient gets while receiving care in a health facility that was not present or incubating at admission — usually appearing **48 hours or more after admission**, or within a set time after discharge or surgery.

**Common HAIs**: catheter-associated urinary tract infection, surgical site infection, ventilator-associated pneumonia, central-line bloodstream infection, and diarrhoea.

**Causes**: poor hand hygiene, invasive devices, contaminated equipment and environment, overuse of antibiotics (resistant organisms), overcrowding, weak patients.

**Prevention**: hand hygiene, standard precautions, aseptic technique, care bundles for catheters and lines, early removal of devices, environmental cleaning, sterilisation of instruments, safe injection practice, staff immunisation, surveillance by the hospital infection control committee and infection control nurse.

## 5.9 Asepsis: medical and surgical

**Asepsis** means freedom from disease-causing micro-organisms.

| | Medical asepsis (clean technique) | Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aim | Reduce the number and spread of micro-organisms | Keep an area or object free of **all** micro-organisms, including spores |
| Used for | Daily care, oral medicines, feeding, bed making | Surgery, catheterisation, injections, dressings of surgical wounds |
| Methods | Hand hygiene, clean gloves, cleaning, disinfection, isolation | Sterile gloves, gowns, instruments, sterile field |

**Definitions**: **cleaning** removes dirt and organic matter; **disinfection** destroys most pathogens but not all spores (for example with alcohol, chlorine, boiling); **sterilisation** destroys all micro-organisms including spores (autoclave — steam under pressure, commonly 121 °C at 15 lb/in² for at least 15 minutes; dry heat; ethylene oxide; plasma). An **antiseptic** is used on living tissue; a **disinfectant** on objects.

**Principles of surgical asepsis**: a sterile object stays sterile only when touched by another sterile object; only sterile items go on a sterile field; a sterile item out of sight or below waist level is considered contaminated; prolonged exposure to air contaminates; moisture passing through a sterile wrapper contaminates by capillary action (strike-through); the 2.5 cm (1 inch) edge of a sterile field is considered unsterile; if in doubt, consider it unsterile.

## 5.10 Hand hygiene

The single most important way to prevent the spread of infection.

**WHO's five moments for hand hygiene**: (1) before touching a patient, (2) before a clean or aseptic procedure, (3) after body fluid exposure risk, (4) after touching a patient, (5) after touching the patient's surroundings.

**Hand rub** (alcohol-based, about 20–30 seconds) is used when hands are not visibly dirty. **Hand washing** with soap and water (about 40–60 seconds) is used when hands are visibly soiled, after using the toilet, and after caring for patients with diarrhoea (for example *Clostridioides difficile*), because alcohol does not kill spores.

**Procedure: hand washing**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Remove rings and watch; nails short; sleeves above the elbows | Micro-organisms collect under jewellery and long nails |
| 2. Wet hands with running water; apply enough soap to cover all surfaces | Running water carries organisms away |
| 3. Rub palm to palm | Friction removes organisms |
| 4. Right palm over the back of the left hand with fingers interlaced, and vice versa | Cleans the backs of the hands |
| 5. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced | Cleans between the fingers |
| 6. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked | Cleans the knuckles |
| 7. Rotational rubbing of each thumb clasped in the other palm | Thumbs are often missed |
| 8. Rotational rubbing of the fingertips in the other palm, backwards and forwards | Cleans fingertips and nails |
| 9. Rinse with hands held so water runs from fingertips to wrists or as per policy; dry with a single-use towel | Removes soap and loosened organisms; wet hands spread organisms more easily |
| 10. Turn off the tap with the towel (or elbow) | Prevents re-contaminating clean hands |

## 5.11 Personal protective equipment (PPE)

PPE includes gloves, gowns or aprons, masks (surgical mask, N95 respirator), eye protection (goggles, face shield), caps and shoe covers. It is chosen by the **expected exposure**, not the diagnosis.

**Order of putting on (donning)**: hand hygiene → gown → mask or respirator → goggles or face shield → gloves (pulled over the gown cuffs).

**Order of taking off (doffing)**: gloves → goggles or face shield → gown → mask or respirator (by the ties, without touching the front) → hand hygiene. (Some protocols remove the gown and gloves together.) The outside of PPE is contaminated; remove it at the doorway and discard it in the correct bin.

## 5.12 Standard precautions

**Standard precautions** are applied to **all patients, at all times**, because any blood or body fluid may be infectious. They include:

1. Hand hygiene.
2. PPE according to the expected exposure.
3. Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette.
4. Safe injection practices; never recap needles by hand; discard sharps immediately into a puncture-proof container.
5. Safe handling of patient care equipment and linen.
6. Environmental cleaning and spill management.
7. Correct patient placement (single room if the patient may contaminate the surroundings).
8. Waste management.
9. Management of needle-stick and splash injuries (wash with soap and water, do not squeeze or suck, report at once for assessment and post-exposure care).

**Transmission-based precautions** are added for known or suspected infections: **contact** (gloves and gown — MRSA, scabies), **droplet** (surgical mask within about 1 metre — influenza, diphtheria) and **airborne** (N95 respirator, negative-pressure or well-ventilated single room — tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox).

## 5.13 Biomedical waste management

**Biomedical waste** is any waste produced during diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of people or animals, or in research. In India it is managed under the **Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016** (with later amendments). Most hospital waste (about 75–90%) is general, non-hazardous waste; the rest is hazardous.

**Types of hospital waste**: general (paper, food, packaging), infectious (soiled dressings, cultures), anatomical (body parts, tissues), sharps (needles, blades), pharmaceutical (expired medicines), chemical (disinfectants, lab chemicals), radioactive, and pressurised containers.

**Colour-coded segregation under the 2016 Rules (summary)**

| Colour | What goes in | Typical treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Yellow** (bag) | Human anatomical waste, animal waste, soiled waste (dressings, cotton, plaster casts, bags contaminated with blood or body fluids), expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste, discarded linen and mattresses, microbiology and lab waste | Incineration, plasma pyrolysis or deep burial (as permitted) |
| **Red** (bag) | Contaminated recyclable waste: tubing, bottles, IV sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, gloves | Autoclaving or microwaving/chemical treatment, then shredding and recycling |
| **White (translucent)** puncture-proof, leak-proof, tamper-proof container | Sharps including metal: needles, syringes with fixed needles, scalpel blades | Autoclaving or dry-heat sterilisation, then shredding or encapsulation |
| **Blue** (puncture-proof box) | Glassware: broken or discarded glass, medicine vials and ampoules (except those contaminated with cytotoxic waste); metallic body implants | Disinfection, then recycling |

General waste goes in a separate (usually black) bin and is handled by the municipal system.

**Rules**: segregate at the **point of generation** (the bedside), fill bags only up to about three-quarters, label with the biohazard symbol, never mix categories, store in a secure place, and send for treatment within the time allowed (untreated waste is not to be stored beyond 48 hours). Staff are trained and immunised against hepatitis B.

**Hazards of poor waste management**: needle-stick injuries and infections (hepatitis B and C, HIV), spread of HAIs, injury to rag-pickers, re-use of discarded syringes, pollution of air, soil and water, and spread of resistant organisms.

**Nurse's role**: segregate correctly, use the right container, never recap needles, report injuries, keep records, and teach junior staff.

## 5.14 Promoting safety: the physical environment

| Factor | What the nurse ensures |
| --- | --- |
| Temperature | Comfortable room temperature; extra warmth for newborns, the elderly and the very ill |
| Humidity | Moderate; very dry air dries mucous membranes, very damp air encourages fungi |
| Ventilation | Fresh air without draughts; windows, exhaust fans — dilutes airborne organisms and odours |
| Light | Good light for work and safety, natural light by day; dim night light for sleep and to prevent falls |
| Noise | Low noise, especially at night; soft voices, oiled trolley wheels, alarms answered quickly |
| Odour | Prompt removal of soiled items, emptying bedpans, ventilation, clean dressings |
| Pest control | Screens, covered food and waste bins, regular pest control (rats, cockroaches, mosquitoes, flies spread disease) |
| Cleanliness | Damp dusting, mopping, clean linen, tidy unit |

## 5.15 Reduction of physical hazards

**Fire**: causes include electrical faults, oxygen use near flames, smoking, and flammable liquids. Prevention: no smoking, checked wiring, "no smoking — oxygen in use" signs, keep exits clear, know where extinguishers are, fire drills.

In a fire follow **RACE**: **R**escue patients in immediate danger, **A**larm (raise the alarm), **C**ontain (close doors and windows, turn off oxygen if safe), **E**xtinguish or Evacuate. To use an extinguisher, remember **PASS**: **P**ull the pin, **A**im at the base of the fire, **S**queeze the handle, **S**weep from side to side. Water is used only for paper, wood and cloth fires, never on electrical fires or burning oil; a carbon dioxide or dry-powder extinguisher is used for electrical fires and flammable liquids. Evacuate horizontally first (to a safe area on the same floor), then down by the stairs, never by lift.

**Other accidents**: electrical shock (check cords, use earthed plugs, dry hands), burns from hot applications, scalds from hot drinks, cuts from sharps, wrong-patient errors (two identifiers, wristbands), medication errors, choking, and patients wandering.

## 5.16 Fall risk assessment

Falls are among the commonest accidents in hospitals. **Risk factors**: age over 65, history of falls, confusion, sedative or blood-pressure medicines, postural hypotension, weakness after illness, poor vision, urinary frequency or urgency, use of walking aids, IV poles, unfamiliar surroundings, wet floors, poor lighting, ill-fitting footwear.

**Assessment tools**: the **Morse Fall Scale** is commonly used. It scores history of falling, a secondary diagnosis, use of an ambulatory aid, an IV line or heparin lock, gait, and mental status; a total of 45 or more indicates high risk (cut-offs may be adjusted by each hospital). Assess on admission, after any change in condition, after a fall, and at regular intervals.

**Prevention**: bed at the lowest level with brakes on, side rails as per policy, call bell and personal items within reach, night light, non-skid slippers, clear walkways, dry floors, grab bars in toilets, help with toileting at regular times, orient the patient to the room, review medicines with the doctor, "fall risk" sign or band, and help to sit up slowly before standing.

**After a fall (post-fall assessment)**: do not lift the patient at once; check responsiveness, airway, breathing, injuries (head, hip); take vital signs; inform the doctor; move safely with help; observe closely for the next 24 hours (especially for head injury); record and complete an incident report; review the care plan.

## 5.17 Safety devices

**Restraints** are physical, chemical (medicines) or environmental methods used to limit a person's movement. They should be the **last resort** after other measures fail.

| Type | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Jacket / vest restraint | Keeps a confused patient in bed or chair |
| Belt restraint | Secures a patient on a stretcher or wheelchair |
| Limb (wrist/ankle) restraint | Prevents pulling out tubes or lines |
| Mitten restraint | Prevents scratching or pulling at dressings |
| Elbow restraint | Stops a child bending the elbow to touch the face (after cleft lip repair) |
| Mummy restraint | Short-term wrap of an infant for a procedure |

**Purposes / indications**: protect patients from injuring themselves or others, prevent removal of tubes and dressings, keep a child still for a procedure — only when less restrictive measures have failed.

**Legal implications and consent**: restraints restrict a person's freedom; wrongly used they can be **false imprisonment** or **assault and battery**. They need a **written order** that states the type, reason and duration, renewed as per policy; **informed consent** from the patient or relative; clear documentation; and the least restrictive method.

**Practice guidelines for applying restraints**

1. Try alternatives first: frequent observation, a family member at the bedside, diversion, treating the cause of confusion.
2. Explain to the patient and family.
3. Use the correct size; pad bony prominences.
4. Tie to the **bed frame**, not the side rail (a rail moves and can injure), with a **quick-release knot** so it can be undone at once in an emergency.
5. Allow **two fingers' space** under the restraint to protect circulation and skin.
6. Check circulation, skin, breathing and position frequently (commonly every 15–30 minutes), and **remove each restraint at regular intervals (about every 2 hours)** for exercise, skin care, toileting, food and fluids.
7. Never restrain a patient flat on the back if they may vomit (risk of aspiration).
8. Document the reason, type, time applied and removed, observations and the patient's response.

**Other safety devices**: side rails (prevent rolling out of bed, but climbing over them can cause worse falls), grab bars in toilets and corridors, call bells and emergency (ambu) alarms, non-skid slippers and mats, bed and wheelchair brakes, bed-exit alarms, wristbands, and low beds.

**Role of the nurse in a safe and clean environment**: assess risks on admission and regularly, keep the unit tidy and well lit, follow infection control and waste rules, check equipment, prevent falls and fires, use restraints correctly, educate patients and families, and report hazards and incidents.

## Remember

- Rubber: cold water, dry, powder, store flat. Glass: rinse in cold water first. Metal: dry to prevent rust.
- Chain of infection: agent → reservoir → portal of exit → transmission → portal of entry → host; break any link.
- Stages of infection: incubation, prodromal, illness, convalescence.
- Inflammation: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.
- HAI: appears 48 hours or more after admission.
- Medical asepsis = clean technique; surgical asepsis = sterile technique (no organisms, including spores).
- WHO five moments; hand rub 20–30 s; hand wash 40–60 s; soap and water for spores and visible soil.
- Donning: gown → mask → goggles → gloves. Doffing: gloves → goggles → gown → mask → hand hygiene.
- BMW Rules 2016: yellow (anatomical, soiled, chemical), red (contaminated plastics), white translucent (sharps), blue (glass).
- Fire: RACE and PASS. Morse Fall Scale: 45 or more = high risk.
- Restraints: last resort, written order, consent, tie to bed frame, quick-release knot, two fingers, release about every 2 hours.

# Unit 6: Comfort, rest and sleep, and pain

INC Unit IX (15 hours theory + 15 hours skill lab): comfort (factors, beds and bed making, therapeutic positions, comfort devices), sleep and rest, and pain (physiology, causes, types, assessment, and drug and non-drug relief, including complementary therapies). Bed making and positions are common OSCE stations.

## 6.1 Comfort

**Comfort** is a state of ease and well-being, physical and mental, in which a person is free of pain and distress. Kolcaba described three forms — **relief** (a specific discomfort is removed), **ease** (calm and contentment) and **transcendence** (rising above problems that cannot be removed) — in four contexts: physical, psychospiritual, social and environmental.

**Factors influencing comfort**

| Group | Factors |
| --- | --- |
| Physical | Pain, nausea, itching, breathlessness, fever, wet or wrinkled linen, uncomfortable position, hunger, a full bladder |
| Psychological | Anxiety, fear, loneliness, embarrassment, lack of information |
| Environmental | Noise, light, temperature, odour, ventilation, cleanliness, crowding |
| Social and cultural | Family support, privacy, respect for customs, food habits |
| Spiritual | Faith, meaning, chance to pray |

Nursing measures: relieve pain, give a clean and well-made bed, correct position and support, hygiene, a calm environment, explanation, privacy, emotional support, and respect for beliefs.

## 6.2 Hospital beds

**Types of beds**

| Bed | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Ordinary (standard) hospital bed | General patients; height adjustable in many models |
| Fowler's bed / backrest bed | Head end can be raised |
| Electric / motorised bed | Height, head and knee sections adjusted by remote — less strain on staff and patient |
| ICU / critical care bed | Multiple positions, side rails, weighing scale, X-ray friendly, CPR release lever |
| Low bed (floor bed) | Patients at high risk of falling |
| Air-fluidised bed, low-air-loss mattress, alternating-pressure air mattress | Prevention and treatment of pressure ulcers, burns |
| Water bed | Spreads pressure evenly |
| Turning frames (e.g. Stryker frame) | Turning patients with spinal injury without bending the spine |
| Bariatric bed | Very heavy patients |
| Paediatric cot / crib | Infants and children, with high sides |

**Purposes of bed making**: comfort and rest; a clean, safe surface; prevent pressure ulcers (smooth, dry, wrinkle-free linen); economise time and linen; keep the ward neat; prepare for a specific patient need (post-operative, fracture, cardiac).

**Principles of bed making**

1. Wash hands; collect all linen in order of use before starting — saves time and energy.
2. Use good body mechanics: raise the bed to working height, wide base, work on one side at a time.
3. Never shake linen, and do not let it touch your uniform or the floor — prevents spread of micro-organisms.
4. Put soiled linen directly into the soiled-linen bag, never on the floor or another bed.
5. Make linen tight and wrinkle-free with **mitred corners** — wrinkles cause pressure and discomfort.
6. Keep the patient covered and warm; give privacy.
7. Finish by lowering the bed, raising side rails if needed, and placing the call bell in reach.

**Mitred (square) corner**: tuck the bottom of the sheet under the mattress at the foot; lift the side edge to form a triangle on the top of the mattress; tuck the hanging lower part under; bring the triangle down and tuck it in. It keeps the sheet firm and neat.

**Types of bed making**

| Type | When used | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Closed bed** | Unoccupied bed waiting for a new admission, or after terminal cleaning | Top sheet and blanket pulled up to the head and covered by the bedspread; keeps the bed clean |
| **Open bed** | Unoccupied bed of a patient who is out of bed (ambulant) or newly admitted and ready to get in | Top covers fan-folded to the foot so the patient can get in easily |
| **Occupied bed** | Patient cannot get out of bed | Patient turned to one side; old linen rolled to the middle, new linen placed on the free half; patient rolled over the "hump" to the clean side; other half completed. Patient covered with a bath blanket throughout |
| **Post-operative (anaesthetic / recovery) bed** | Receiving a patient from the operation theatre | Top covers fan-folded to the far side (or the foot) for an easy transfer; mackintosh and draw sheet at the head end to protect from vomit; pillows removed or placed upright at the head to protect from injury; equipment at hand — kidney tray, tongue depressor, mouth gag, suction, oxygen, BP apparatus, airway, warm blankets |
| **Cardiac bed** | Heart failure, breathlessness | Backrest and pillows so the patient sits up (Fowler's or orthopnoeic position); cardiac (over-bed) table with a pillow to lean on; knee support and footrest to prevent sliding |
| **Fracture bed** | Fractures of the spine, pelvis, lower limbs | **Fracture boards** placed under the mattress so it does not sag; bed cradle to keep the weight of covers off the limb; traction equipment if ordered |
| **Amputation bed** | After amputation of a lower limb | Divided top covers so the stump can be watched for bleeding; bed cradle; sandbags; tourniquet kept at hand as per protocol |
| **Burns bed** | Burns | Sterile linen, bed cradle to keep covers off the burnt area, warm room |

**Procedure: occupied bed (main steps with rationale)**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Check the patient's condition and any restrictions (drains, traction, position) | Prevents harm |
| 2. Explain; screen; close windows | Co-operation, privacy, prevents chill |
| 3. Arrange clean linen on a chair in order of use | Saves time |
| 4. Loosen linen all round; replace the top sheet with a bath blanket | Keeps the patient covered and warm |
| 5. Turn the patient to the far side, with the side rail up on that side | Safety |
| 6. Roll soiled linen towards the patient's back; clean and dry the mattress; place clean sheet and draw sheet on the free half and roll the rest towards the patient | Works one half at a time |
| 7. Turn the patient over the roll to the clean side; remove the soiled linen into the linen bag; pull the clean linen through and tuck it tightly | Wrinkle-free bottom sheet prevents pressure areas |
| 8. Change the pillow cover; place the top sheet and blanket; remove the bath blanket from beneath; make a toe pleat | Toe pleat leaves room for the feet and prevents foot drop |
| 9. Make the patient comfortable; bed low, side rails up as needed, call bell in reach | Safety and comfort |
| 10. Remove linen bag; wash hands; record | Infection control; communication |

## 6.3 Therapeutic positions

| Position | Description | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Supine (dorsal)** | Lying flat on the back, head on a pillow | Rest, examination of the front of the body, after spinal anaesthesia (as ordered) |
| **Dorsal recumbent** | On the back with knees bent and feet flat on the bed | Perineal care, vaginal examination, catheterisation of women, inserting a rectal tube |
| **Fowler's** | Head of bed raised: low 15–30°, semi 30–45°, high 60–90° | Breathlessness, heart failure, after thyroid and abdominal surgery, feeding, drainage of the abdomen |
| **Orthopnoeic** | Sitting up, leaning forward over an over-bed table with a pillow | Severe breathlessness (asthma, heart failure) — lets the chest expand fully |
| **Prone** | Lying on the abdomen, head turned to one side | Examination of the back, after some spine surgery, drainage from the mouth, some respiratory distress protocols |
| **Lateral (side-lying)** | On the side with upper hip and knee flexed | Rest, relieving pressure on the back and sacrum, giving an enema (left lateral) |
| **Sims' (semi-prone)** | Left side with the right knee drawn up towards the chest, left arm behind the back | Enemas, rectal examination, vaginal examination, unconscious patient (drainage of secretions) |
| **Trendelenburg** | Bed tilted so the head is lower than the feet | Some pelvic surgery; formerly for shock (now raise legs only, as ordered) |
| **Reverse Trendelenburg** | Feet lower than the head | Reduces reflux, some neck and head surgery |
| **Lithotomy** | On the back with hips and knees flexed and legs in stirrups | Childbirth, vaginal and perineal procedures, cystoscopy |
| **Knee–chest (genupectoral)** | Kneeling with chest on the bed, hips raised | Rectal examination, sigmoidoscopy, to relieve pressure of a prolapsed cord (as ordered) |

**Guidelines**: change position at least every 2 hours for a bed-bound patient; support joints in good alignment; pad bony prominences; check skin and comfort; explain and give privacy; record the position and time.

## 6.4 Comfort devices

| Device | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Pillows | Support, alignment, elevation of a limb, comfort |
| Backrest | Supports the patient in a sitting or Fowler's position |
| Cardiac (over-bed) table | Support for leaning forward (orthopnoea), meals, writing |
| Bed cradle | Keeps the weight of bed covers off the legs or a burn or fracture site |
| Footboard / foot rest | Keeps feet at a right angle, prevents foot drop and sliding down the bed |
| Sandbags | Support a limb and prevent rotation; keep a part still |
| Trochanter roll | Rolled towel along the thigh to prevent external rotation of the hip |
| Hand roll | Keeps fingers in a functional position |
| Air cushion / ring cushion | Relieves pressure (ring cushions are now discouraged for pressure areas as they can reduce blood flow) |
| Special mattresses | Air, water, foam — spread weight to prevent pressure ulcers |
| Knee rest / bolster | Supports the knees, prevents sliding |
| Side rails | Safety |

## 6.5 Sleep and rest

**Rest** is a state of mental and physical calmness and relaxation. **Sleep** is a natural, recurring state of reduced awareness and response, from which a person can be woken.

**Physiology of sleep**: sleep is controlled by the **reticular activating system** in the brainstem (keeps us awake) and the **bulbar synchronising region** (promotes sleep). The **circadian rhythm** (about 24-hour body clock), set by daylight through the hypothalamus and the hormone **melatonin** from the pineal gland, decides when we feel sleepy.

**Stages of sleep**: sleep has two kinds, **non-REM** and **REM** (rapid eye movement).

| Stage | Features |
| --- | --- |
| NREM stage 1 (N1) | Very light sleep, a few minutes; easily woken; drifting feeling |
| NREM stage 2 (N2) | Light sleep; body relaxes further; heart rate and temperature fall |
| NREM stage 3 (N3, deep or slow-wave sleep) | Deepest sleep; hard to wake; body repair, growth hormone release; sleep-walking and bed-wetting happen here |
| REM sleep | Vivid dreams, rapid eye movements, muscles very relaxed, irregular pulse and breathing; important for memory and mood |

```text
Awake → N1 → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM → N2 → N3 … (one cycle ≈ 90 minutes; 4–6 cycles a night)
REM periods get longer towards morning.
```

**Sleep needs by age (approximate)**: newborns sleep most of the day (about 16 hours), children about 10–12 hours, adolescents about 8–10, adults about 7–8, older adults similar but with lighter, more broken sleep.

**Factors affecting sleep**: illness (pain, breathlessness, frequent urination), hospital environment (noise, lights, procedures at night, strange bed), anxiety and depression, lifestyle (shift work, late meals, caffeine, alcohol, smoking), medicines (diuretics, steroids, sedatives — sedatives can reduce REM sleep), exercise and fatigue, diet, age.

**Promoting rest and sleep**

1. Assess the patient's usual sleep pattern and bedtime routine.
2. Keep the environment quiet, dark and at a comfortable temperature; dim lights at night; group night-time care so the patient is disturbed less.
3. Encourage a bedtime routine: warm bath, light snack or warm milk, prayer, reading.
4. Relieve pain and discomfort before sleep; comfortable position, clean dry bed, empty bladder.
5. Avoid caffeine and heavy meals in the evening; limit daytime naps.
6. Relaxation techniques: deep breathing, back rub (massage), soft music.
7. Reduce anxiety by explaining and listening.
8. Give sleep medicines only as prescribed and observe their effect.

**Sleep disorders**

| Disorder | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Insomnia | Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early; the most common |
| Hypersomnia | Excessive sleep or daytime sleepiness |
| Narcolepsy | Sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep during the day, sometimes with sudden muscle weakness (cataplexy) |
| Sleep apnoea | Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep; loud snoring, daytime sleepiness; obstructive type is common in obese people |
| Sleep deprivation | Not enough sleep — irritability, poor concentration, confusion |
| Parasomnias | Unusual behaviour during sleep: sleep-walking (somnambulism), night terrors, nightmares, bed-wetting (enuresis), teeth grinding (bruxism), sleep talking |

## 6.6 Pain

**Pain** is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. Margo McCaffery's nursing definition: pain is **whatever the person says it is, existing whenever they say it does**. The nurse therefore **believes the patient's report**.

**Physiology of pain (nociception)**

| Process | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Transduction | Injury releases chemicals (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, substance P) that stimulate pain receptors (nociceptors) |
| Transmission | The impulse travels along A-delta fibres (fast, sharp, well-localised pain) and C fibres (slow, dull, aching pain) to the spinal cord and up to the thalamus and brain |
| Perception | The brain (cortex) becomes aware of pain and its meaning |
| Modulation | The body changes the signal — endorphins and descending pathways reduce it |

**Gate control theory** (Melzack and Wall, 1965): a "gate" in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord controls how many pain signals reach the brain. Large-fibre stimulation (rubbing, massage, TENS, heat and cold) and positive thoughts close the gate; anxiety and fear open it. This explains why non-drug measures work.

**Common causes of pain**: tissue injury (trauma, surgery, burns), inflammation, infection, ischaemia (angina), obstruction or stretching of hollow organs (renal stone, distended bladder), muscle spasm, nerve damage, tumours, and psychological factors.

**Types of pain**

| Basis | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Duration | **Acute** (sudden, short, a known cause, protective; fast pulse, sweating) and **chronic** (lasts beyond about three months or beyond normal healing; may cause depression, fatigue) |
| Origin | **Cutaneous** (skin, sharp, burning), **deep somatic** (bones, muscles, diffuse), **visceral** (organs, poorly localised, cramping) |
| Spread | **Radiating** (spreads from the source), **referred** (felt away from the source — heart pain in the left arm, gallbladder pain in the right shoulder) |
| Cause | **Nociceptive** (tissue damage), **neuropathic** (nerve damage — burning, shooting), **phantom** (felt in an amputated part), **psychogenic** (no physical cause found, but the pain is real), **intractable** (resists treatment) |

## 6.7 Pain assessment

Ask about pain at every assessment (the "fifth vital sign"). A common memory aid is **PQRST**:

| Letter | Question |
| --- | --- |
| P — Provoking / palliating | What brings it on, makes it worse or better? |
| Q — Quality | What does it feel like — sharp, dull, burning, throbbing? |
| R — Region / radiation | Where is it? Does it spread? |
| S — Severity | How bad is it on a scale of 0 to 10? |
| T — Timing | When did it start, how long does it last, is it constant or on and off? |

Also note its effect on sleep, appetite, mood and activity, what the patient has tried, and **non-verbal signs**: facial grimace, guarding, crying, restlessness, rapid pulse, raised BP, sweating.

**Pain scales**

| Scale | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Numeric rating scale (NRS) | 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst possible); adults who can count |
| Visual analogue scale (VAS) | A 10 cm line; patient marks the point matching their pain |
| Verbal descriptor scale | None, mild, moderate, severe, very severe |
| Wong–Baker FACES scale | Faces from smiling to crying; children (about 3 years and older), people with language barriers |
| FLACC scale | Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability — for young children and non-verbal patients |
| Behavioural scales | For confused, sedated or unconscious patients |

**Sedation ("narcotic") scales**: patients receiving opioid (narcotic) pain medicines are also checked for sedation, because excess sedation comes before breathing slows. A commonly used tool is the **Pasero Opioid-induced Sedation Scale**: S = normal sleep, easy to wake; 1 = awake and alert; 2 = slightly drowsy, easily roused; 3 = frequently drowsy, drifts off during conversation; 4 = very sleepy, minimal or no response. Levels 3 and 4 are unacceptable — stop the opioid, stay with the patient, check breathing and SpO2, and inform the doctor at once. Respiratory rate and depth are recorded with the sedation level.

## 6.8 Pain-relieving measures

**A. Pharmacological (drug) measures** — given only as prescribed. The **WHO analgesic ladder** guides cancer pain: step 1 non-opioid (paracetamol, NSAIDs) ± adjuvant; step 2 weak opioid ± non-opioid ± adjuvant; step 3 strong opioid ± non-opioid ± adjuvant. Adjuvants include some antidepressants and anticonvulsants for nerve pain. Giving analgesics **by the clock** (regularly) controls continuous pain better than waiting until pain returns.

**Use of narcotics (opioids)**: they are effective for severe pain but can cause sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, nausea and itching, and they are controlled drugs.

- Check the prescription, the patient's pain and sedation level and respiratory rate before each dose.
- Store them under double lock; keep a register; count the stock at each shift; a second nurse witnesses giving and discarding of unused drug, as per hospital and legal rules (the NDPS Act controls narcotic drugs in India).
- Prevent constipation with fluids, fibre and prescribed laxatives.
- Fear of addiction should not stop proper pain relief; addiction is uncommon when opioids are used correctly for pain.

**Principles of safe medicine administration (the "rights")**: every pain medicine is given with the rights checked — **right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time, right documentation**, and also the right reason, right response (evaluate the effect) and the patient's right to know and to refuse. Doses are always as prescribed; nurses never decide them.

**Routes used for pain relief**: oral (first choice when the patient can swallow), sublingual or buccal, rectal, transdermal (patch), subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous, epidural and intrathecal (spinal), and local or regional (nerve blocks, local anaesthetic infiltration). After a dose, reassess pain (commonly about 30 minutes after an injection and about an hour after an oral dose, or as per protocol) and record the response.

**Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)**: a programmed pump that lets the patient press a button to receive a small preset dose of an analgesic, usually intravenously. A **lockout interval** prevents another dose too soon, and a maximum limit is set. Benefits: quick relief, patient control, less anxiety. Only the patient should press the button (not relatives — risk of overdose). Monitor pain, sedation, breathing and the pump record.

**TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation)**: a small battery device sends mild electrical currents through skin electrodes placed near the painful area. It works by the gate control mechanism and possibly endorphin release. Used for back pain, post-operative pain and labour pain. Not used over the front of the neck, eyes, broken skin, or in people with a pacemaker.

**Invasive techniques of pain management**: epidural analgesia (catheter in the epidural space), intrathecal (spinal) analgesia, nerve blocks with local anaesthetic, local infiltration of wounds, and, rarely for intractable pain, surgical procedures that interrupt nerve pathways. Nurses monitor the insertion site, sensation and movement of the legs, BP, breathing and sedation.

**Newer measures**: wound catheters that infuse local anaesthetic, long-acting local anaesthetic preparations, nerve stimulators, virtual reality distraction, and structured pain management services.

**B. Non-pharmacological measures**

| Measure | How it helps |
| --- | --- |
| Positioning, support, a comfortable bed | Removes pressure and strain |
| Heat and cold applications | Relax muscles / numb and reduce swelling |
| Massage (back rub) | Relaxation; closes the "gate" |
| Distraction (music, TV, conversation, games) | Shifts attention from pain |
| Relaxation and deep breathing | Reduces muscle tension and anxiety |
| Guided imagery | Patient imagines a pleasant scene |
| Splinting the wound when coughing | Reduces pull on the incision |
| Information and reassurance | Reduces fear, which magnifies pain |
| Presence and touch | Comfort and trust |

**C. Complementary and alternative therapies (CAM)**: therapies used alongside (complementary) or instead of (alternative) standard treatment — **yoga, meditation, acupressure, acupuncture, aromatherapy, music therapy, therapeutic touch, reflexology, hypnosis**, and **AYUSH** systems (Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy). The nurse asks about their use, supports safe practices the patient values, and tells the doctor about any herbal products (some interact with medicines).

## Remember

- Comfort: relief, ease, transcendence.
- Closed bed = waiting for admission; open bed = ambulant patient; occupied bed = patient in bed; post-operative bed = covers fan-folded, vomit protection, emergency equipment ready; fracture bed = fracture boards and bed cradle; cardiac bed = sitting up with backrest and cardiac table.
- Mitred corner keeps sheets tight; never shake linen.
- Fowler's: low 15–30°, semi 30–45°, high 60–90°. Sims' = left side, right knee up (enema). Lithotomy = legs in stirrups. Dorsal recumbent = knees bent, feet flat.
- Sleep: NREM N1–N3 + REM; cycle about 90 minutes; melatonin and circadian rhythm.
- Pain is what the patient says it is; assess with PQRST and a scale (NRS, FACES, FLACC).
- Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965): massage, TENS, heat and cold close the gate.
- WHO ladder: non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid, ± adjuvants.
- Opioids: check pain, sedation and breathing; double-lock storage; register.
- PCA: lockout interval; only the patient presses the button.
- Medication rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation (+ reason, response, right to refuse).

# Unit 7: Admission and discharge, mobility and immobility, patient education

INC Unit XI (6 hours theory + 2 skill lab): hospital admission and discharge. INC Unit XII (8 hours theory + 10 skill lab): mobility and immobility. INC Unit XIII (4 hours theory + 2 skill lab): patient education. They are joined because together they follow a patient from arrival, through care in bed and getting moving again, to going home well prepared.

## 7.1 Admission to the hospital

**Admission** is accepting a patient into a hospital ward for observation, diagnosis or treatment. It may be **routine (planned / elective)**, for example for planned surgery, or **emergency**, through the casualty department.

The first impression matters: a warm, organised admission reduces anxiety and builds trust.

**Preparation of the unit**

1. Get information about the incoming patient (diagnosis, condition, age, sex, any special needs).
2. Prepare the **admission bed**: a clean **closed bed** converted to an **open bed** when the patient arrives (or a post-operative bed or other special bed if needed); mackintosh and draw sheet as needed.
3. Check the unit: locker, over-bed table, chair, call bell, light, oxygen and suction points working.
4. Keep ready the admission tray: thermometer, BP apparatus, stethoscope, weighing machine, measuring tape, urine specimen container, identity band, admission forms, patient gown.

**Admission procedure**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Greet the patient and family by name; introduce yourself | Reduces anxiety; shows respect |
| 2. Check identity and the admission papers; put on an **identification band** with at least two identifiers (name and hospital number) | Prevents errors throughout the stay |
| 3. Take the patient to the bed; help change into a hospital gown if required; give privacy | Comfort and dignity |
| 4. **Orient** the patient and family to the ward: bed controls, call bell, toilet, visiting hours, meal times, rules, the nurse in charge | Reduces fear of the unfamiliar; promotes safety |
| 5. Record **vital signs, height and weight** and collect any ordered specimens | Baseline values for comparison |
| 6. Take the **nursing history** and do an initial assessment (including allergies, current medicines, fall risk, pressure ulcer risk, pain) | Basis for the nursing care plan |
| 7. Take care of **valuables and belongings**: list them, give to relatives or to the hospital locker against a signed receipt | Prevents loss and disputes |
| 8. Inform the doctor; carry out admission orders | Starts treatment promptly |
| 9. Explain the plan, tests and what to expect; answer questions | Knowledge reduces anxiety |
| 10. **Record** the admission: date, time, mode (walking, wheelchair, stretcher), condition, vital signs, belongings, care given | Legal record and communication |

**Medico-legal issues at admission**

- **Medico-legal cases (MLC)**: accidents, assault, burns, poisoning, suspected suicide or homicide, sexual offences, unknown or unconscious patients brought by police — the doctor registers an MLC and informs the police as per law; the nurse preserves evidence (clothes, specimens, vomitus) in labelled, sealed containers, records exact times and facts, and maintains the chain of custody.
- **Consent**: general consent for admission and treatment; **informed consent** (written) for procedures and surgery, signed by the patient or, if the patient is a minor or cannot decide, by the legal guardian.
- **Emergency care** must not be delayed for paperwork.
- Accurate identification, honest records, privacy and confidentiality.

**Roles and responsibilities of the nurse in admission**: welcoming and orienting, safe identification, baseline assessment, safe custody of belongings, informing the doctor, starting the care plan, emotional support, health teaching from day one, and complete documentation.

## 7.2 Discharge, referral and transfer

**Discharge** is the release of a patient from the hospital.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Planned discharge** | The doctor decides the patient is fit to go; prepared in advance |
| **LAMA (Leave Against Medical Advice)** / DAMA | Patient or family decides to leave although the doctor advises staying. The nurse informs the doctor, the doctor explains the risks, and the patient or guardian signs a LAMA form; record everything. The patient cannot be kept by force (except under specific legal provisions) |
| **Abscond** | Patient leaves without informing anyone. Search the premises, inform the nurse in charge, the doctor and security; inform the family and, in medico-legal cases, the police; record the time last seen and the facts |
| **Referral** | Sent to another specialist or hospital for care not available here |
| **Transfer** | Moved to another ward, unit or hospital (internal or external) |
| **Death** | Discharge by death — last offices and handing over the body as per policy |

**Discharge planning**

Discharge planning **starts on the day of admission**. It aims to make the move home safe and to prevent readmission. It includes:

1. Assessing what the patient and family will need at home (self-care ability, support, home conditions, money).
2. Teaching medicines, diet, wound care, exercises, warning signs, and when to come back.
3. Arranging equipment (walker, wheelchair), home care or community nurse follow-up.
4. Co-ordinating with the doctor, physiotherapist, dietitian and social worker.
5. Giving written instructions in a language the patient understands.

A common memory aid is **METHOD**: **M**edications, **E**nvironment (home safety), **T**reatment (wound care, exercises), **H**ealth teaching, **O**utpatient follow-up, **D**iet.

**Discharge procedure**

1. Check the written discharge order.
2. Inform the patient and family in advance; plan transport.
3. Complete teaching; check understanding (ask the patient to explain back).
4. Give the discharge summary, prescriptions, investigation reports, follow-up date and instructions.
5. Return the patient's valuables and medicines brought from home against signature.
6. Remove IV lines or other devices as ordered.
7. Complete billing formalities as per hospital procedure.
8. Take the patient to the vehicle by wheelchair if needed.
9. Record the date, time, condition, mode of leaving, who accompanied, and the instructions given.
10. Inform the admission office; prepare the unit.

**Transfer procedure**: check the order; inform the receiving unit and family; prepare the patient; give a transfer report (condition, vital signs, medicines last given, allergies, pending tests); send records and belongings; accompany a seriously ill patient; record.

**Medico-legal issues at discharge**: LAMA forms, discharge of MLC patients only with proper documentation and police intimation where required, correct handing over of minors to their guardians, accurate discharge summaries, and confidentiality of records.

**Care of the unit after discharge (terminal cleaning)**: strip the bed, send linen to the laundry (infected linen separately), clean and disinfect the mattress, bed, locker and equipment as per the infection control policy (more thoroughly after infectious patients), air the room, make a closed bed, and replace equipment.

## 7.3 Mobility: elements of normal movement

**Mobility** is the ability to move freely, easily and purposefully. It depends on:

| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Body alignment and posture** | Body parts in correct relation to one another; the line of gravity passes through the base of support |
| **Joint mobility** | Range of motion (ROM) of each joint |
| **Balance** | Keeping the body stable; the centre of gravity stays over the base of support |
| **Coordinated movement** | Smooth, purposeful movement through nerves, muscles and bones working together |

## 7.4 Principles of body mechanics

**Body mechanics** is the efficient, safe use of the body during activity. It protects nurses from back injury and patients from harm.

1. **Wide base of support** (feet apart, one slightly forward) — more stability.
2. **Lower the centre of gravity** (bend the knees and hips, not the back).
3. **Keep the object or patient close** to your body — less strain on the back.
4. **Use the large leg and arm muscles**, not the back.
5. **Face the direction of movement**; turn by pivoting the feet, **do not twist the spine**.
6. **Push, pull or roll rather than lift** where possible; slide on a smooth surface (draw sheet, slide sheet).
7. **Work at a comfortable height** — raise the bed.
8. **Tighten the abdominal and gluteal muscles** before moving — supports the spine.
9. **Get help** or use mechanical aids (hoists) for heavy or dependent patients; move on a count so everyone acts together.

## 7.5 Factors affecting body alignment and activity

Age and development, health status (pain, fractures, paralysis, arthritis, heart and lung disease), nutrition (obesity, malnutrition), emotions (depression, fear of falling), lifestyle and occupation, medicines (sedatives), pregnancy, and environment (stairs, slippery floors).

## 7.6 Exercise: types and benefits

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isotonic (dynamic) | Muscle shortens and moves a joint | Walking, swimming, ROM exercises |
| Isometric (static) | Muscle tightens without moving the joint | Quadriceps setting, gluteal setting in bed |
| Isokinetic | Movement against a constant resistance on a machine | Physiotherapy equipment |
| Aerobic | Uses oxygen; continuous large-muscle activity | Brisk walking, cycling |
| Anaerobic | Short bursts without enough oxygen | Weight lifting, sprinting |

**ROM exercises**: **active** (patient does them independently), **active-assisted** (patient does with help), **passive** (nurse or therapist moves the joint for a patient who cannot).

**Benefits of exercise**: stronger heart and better circulation, better lung expansion, maintained muscle strength and joint flexibility, stronger bones, better digestion and bowel movement, weight control, better sleep, better mood and self-esteem, lower risk of diabetes and high BP.

## 7.7 Effects of immobility

| System | Effects |
| --- | --- |
| Skin | **Pressure ulcers** (over the sacrum, heels, hips, elbows, back of head) |
| Musculoskeletal | Muscle wasting (atrophy) and weakness, **contractures** (foot drop, hip and knee flexion), joint stiffness, **osteoporosis** (calcium loss from bone) |
| Cardiovascular | **Orthostatic hypotension**, more work for the heart, **deep vein thrombosis** (slow venous flow) and pulmonary embolism, dependent oedema |
| Respiratory | Shallow breathing, collection of secretions, **hypostatic pneumonia**, atelectasis |
| Gastrointestinal | Loss of appetite, **constipation**, indigestion |
| Urinary | Urinary stasis, **infection**, **kidney stones** (from calcium loss), retention |
| Metabolic | Lower metabolism, negative nitrogen balance, calcium loss |
| Psychological | Boredom, depression, loss of self-esteem, sleep disturbance, confusion (especially in the elderly) |

## 7.8 Maintaining body alignment and activity: nursing interventions

**Assessment**: posture and alignment, gait, ROM, muscle strength, balance, activity tolerance, pain, skin, and risk scores for falls and pressure ulcers.

**Maintaining alignment (positions)**: support each position with pillows and devices — head in line with the spine, hips and knees slightly flexed, feet at a right angle against a footboard, trochanter roll to prevent outward rotation of the hip, hand roll for the fingers; change position at least every 2 hours.

**Moving a patient up in bed (two nurses)**: explain; bed flat and raised, brakes on; remove the pillow and place it at the head of the bed (protects the head); patient flexes the knees and pushes with the feet if able; nurses on each side hold the draw (lift) sheet close to the patient; wide stance facing the head of the bed; on a count of three, slide the patient up (do not drag on the skin — causes friction injury); replace the pillow and make comfortable.

**Turning to the side (log rolling** for spinal injury: two or three nurses turn the head, shoulders and hips together, keeping the spine straight).

**Assisting to sit at the edge of the bed (dangling)**: raise the head of the bed, swing the legs over the side while supporting the shoulders, let the patient sit for a minute and check for dizziness (orthostatic hypotension) before standing.

**Transferring from bed to wheelchair**

| Step | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Place the wheelchair at an angle of about 45° to the bed on the patient's **stronger side**; lock the brakes; lift the footrests away | Short pivot; stability; the strong side leads |
| 2. Lower the bed; help the patient sit on the edge; put on non-skid footwear | Feet flat on the floor; prevents slipping |
| 3. Stand in front with a wide base and bent knees; use a gait belt if available | Body mechanics; secure hold |
| 4. On a count, help the patient stand, pivot on the strong foot and sit down in the chair | Coordinated movement; less strain |
| 5. Position the feet on the footrests, cover the legs, give the call bell | Comfort and safety |

**Bed to stretcher**: bring the stretcher alongside at the same height, lock both, use a slide sheet or roller board, at least three people (more for heavy patients), move on a count, side rails up, cover the patient.

**Lifting**: use mechanical hoists for dependent patients; avoid manual lifting of the full body weight where possible.

## 7.9 Walking and assisting with ambulation

**Ambulation** is walking. Early ambulation after surgery or illness prevents many effects of immobility.

- Check vital signs and dizziness before walking; let the patient sit first.
- Non-skid footwear, clear path, good light.
- Walk at the patient's **weaker side**, holding a gait belt or with one arm around the waist, so you can support them.
- If the patient faints or starts to fall, **ease them gently to the floor** while protecting the head — do not try to hold them up.

**Walking aids**

| Aid | Guidelines |
| --- | --- |
| **Cane (walking stick)** | Held in the hand on the **stronger** side; top at the level of the hip (greater trochanter); elbow slightly bent. Move the cane and the weak leg together, then the strong leg |
| **Walker** | Lift (or roll) the walker forward, step into it with the weak leg, then the strong leg; do not walk too close to the front bar |
| **Crutches (axillary)** | Top of the crutch about 3 finger-widths (a few centimetres) below the axilla; elbows slightly bent; **weight is taken on the hands, never on the armpits** (pressure damages the axillary nerves and vessels — crutch palsy) |

**Crutch gaits**: four-point (slowest, most stable: right crutch, left foot, left crutch, right foot), three-point (both crutches with the injured leg, then the good leg — when one leg cannot bear weight), two-point (crutch and opposite foot together — faster), swing-to and swing-through (both legs swing to or past the crutches — for paraplegics with braces). On stairs: "up with the good, down with the bad" (going up, the good leg leads; going down, the crutches and injured leg lead).

## 7.10 Care of patients with immobility using the nursing process

| Step | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Assessment | Mobility level, skin condition, muscle strength, ROM, breathing, bowel and bladder, mood, risk scores |
| Nursing diagnosis | Impaired physical mobility related to a fracture; risk for impaired skin integrity related to immobility; risk for constipation |
| Planning | Patient will keep skin intact; will do ROM exercises twice a day; will walk with a walker within one week |
| Implementation | Turning every 2 hours, pressure-relieving mattress, skin care, ROM and breathing exercises, coughing, fluids and fibre, early mobilisation, diversion, teaching |
| Evaluation | Skin intact, no contractures, chest clear, regular bowel movement, walking distance increasing |

## 7.11 Care of patients with casts and splints

A **cast** is a rigid casing (plaster of Paris or fibreglass) that keeps a fractured bone still. A **splint** is a support, often removable, used for immobilisation and first aid.

**Care of a patient with a cast**

| Care | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| Support a wet plaster cast on pillows; handle with the **palms**, not fingertips; leave it uncovered to dry (plaster takes a day or more to dry fully; fibreglass sets quickly) | Fingertips make dents that press on the skin; covering slows drying |
| Elevate the limb above heart level for the first days | Reduces swelling |
| Do **neurovascular checks** often (especially the first 24–48 hours): the **5 Ps — pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia (tingling, numbness), paralysis** — plus colour, warmth, capillary refill and swelling of fingers or toes | Detects compartment syndrome and pressure from a tight cast early |
| **Pain that is not relieved by prescribed analgesia, or increases on passive stretching of the fingers or toes, must be reported at once** | It may be compartment syndrome — an emergency |
| Check the cast edges; petal them with tape if rough | Prevents skin abrasion |
| Never insert objects inside the cast to scratch; report a bad smell, drainage or hot spots | Prevents skin injury; signs of infection or pressure ulcer |
| Keep the cast dry (cover with plastic when bathing) | A wet plaster cast softens |
| Exercise unaffected joints; isometric exercises of muscles inside the cast as advised | Prevents stiffness and wasting |
| Teach the patient and family these points before discharge | Safe home care |

**Splints**: check that they are well padded and not too tight, check skin and circulation, and teach correct application if removable.

## 7.12 Patient education

**Patient teaching** is a planned process of helping patients and families gain the knowledge, attitudes and skills they need to maintain or improve health. It is a legal and professional responsibility of the nurse.

**Importance and purposes**: promote health and prevent illness, help patients cope with illness and treatment, improve self-care and adherence to treatment, shorten hospital stay and prevent readmission, reduce anxiety and complications, and involve families in care.

**Domains of learning** (Bloom)

| Domain | What is learnt | Teaching method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cognitive | Knowledge and understanding | Explanation, discussion, leaflets |
| Affective | Attitudes, values, feelings | Discussion, role play, sharing experiences |
| Psychomotor | Skills | **Demonstration and return demonstration** (e.g. using an inhaler, checking blood sugar) |

**Principles of teaching**: assess readiness and motivation; start from what the patient already knows; teach from simple to complex; use the patient's language and simple words; short sessions; involve the patient actively; use more than one sense (see, hear, do); repeat key points; give written material; reinforce with praise; involve the family; choose a time free of pain and fatigue.

**Process of patient teaching (integrating the nursing process)**

| Step | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Assessment | Learning needs, readiness, literacy, language, culture, physical and emotional state, support at home |
| Nursing diagnosis | Deficient knowledge related to a new diagnosis of diabetes |
| Planning | Set measurable learning objectives with the patient (e.g. "will demonstrate insulin pen use correctly before discharge"); choose content, method, materials, time |
| Implementation | Teach, demonstrate, involve the family, give leaflets |
| Evaluation | Ask the patient to explain in their own words (**teach-back**) or do a return demonstration; re-teach what was missed; document what was taught and the response |

**Barriers to learning**: pain, anxiety, fatigue, low literacy, language difference, hearing or vision problems, cultural beliefs, denial, a noisy environment, and lack of time.

## Remember

- Admission: welcome, ID band (two identifiers), orient, baseline vital signs and weight, history, valuables listed and signed, inform doctor, record.
- MLC: preserve evidence, record facts and times, police informed by the doctor as per law.
- Discharge planning starts at admission; METHOD = Medications, Environment, Treatment, Health teaching, Outpatient follow-up, Diet.
- LAMA: inform doctor, explain risks, signed LAMA form, record. Abscond: search, inform, record.
- Terminal cleaning of the unit after discharge.
- Body mechanics: wide base, low centre of gravity, load close, use legs, pivot don't twist, push rather than lift.
- Isotonic = moves joint; isometric = tightens without moving.
- Immobility: pressure ulcers, contractures, osteoporosis, DVT, orthostatic hypotension, hypostatic pneumonia, constipation, UTI and stones, depression.
- Wheelchair at 45° on the strong side, brakes locked. Walk on the weak side. Cane in the strong hand.
- Crutches: weight on the hands, not the axillae; up with the good, down with the bad.
- Cast: handle with palms, elevate, 5 Ps, report unrelieved pain (compartment syndrome).
- Teaching: cognitive, affective, psychomotor; return demonstration and teach-back.
